Energy eigenvalues for N-dimensional harmonic oscillators have been calculated in closed form for specific cases of three types of anisotropic momentum potentials. These calculations demonstrate that the proposed technique is capable of handling challenges related to convergence, parameter dependence, and finite-baryonic-chemical-potential. Building on these findings, the theoretical framework for describing quarkonium bound states in N-dimensional space with anisotropic momentum has been established. Using the theoretical weak interaction potential, energy eigenvalues for quarkonium bound states such as $J/\psi$, $\chi_{c1}$, and $\Upsilon$ were calculated. These calculations show that ANI contributes positively to the dissociation of quarkonia at low temperatures, but negatively at high temperatures. Furthermore, the theoretical predictions indicate that the dissociation of $J / \psi$ is less affected by ANI and density compared to $\Upsilon$, with the reverse true for $\chi_{c1}$.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and DhRuO7 using neutron powder diffraction. We found that Tb3RuO7 exhibits a unique combination of an alternating bond chain of Ru spins that partially disordered due to thermal effects, along with the simultaneous occurrence of Dy spins that are coupled to rare earth ions. Notably, Tb and Ru ions in Tb3RuO7 are located at symmetry-equivalent positions, causing it to have identical unit cell dimensions as the $Uce521c$ structure of Dy3RuO7. Furthermore, Tb and Dy ions in Tb3RuO7 and DhRuO7 are subjected to a special type of magnetic field that is oriented along the c-axis. This duality of magnetic fields causes the rare earth ions to localize on rare earth sites, leading to a phenomenon where they become frozen at temperatures above 12 K in Tb3RuO7 and 17 K in DhRuO7. To better understand this magnetic arrangement, we proposed a model that considers the impact of rare earth ions that localize on rare earth sites on/dy other ions that reside at equivalent positions in a head tail type of magnetic field.

Many complex systems, such as those through which light passes, can be understood by analyzing the periodic properties of the data. While deep learning models have shown potential in this area by using data-driven approaches, their reliance on vast amounts of data and the limited capabilities of current convolutional neural networks for capturing phase and frequency information are significant hindrances. Our proposed solution is a new local periodic activation function based on the 1D discrete cosine transform that can capture the underlying characteristics of data within specific segments. When combined with the unique em modulation technique, our model is able to encode local frequencies, phases, and coefficients, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying properties of the data. Moreover, our approach's ability to resynthesize the original data from periodic segments with minimal distortion allows it to generate the most accurate periodic representation. Moreover, our model's ability to generalize across different classes of data is evident from its ability to perform well on new datasets with only periodic signals of that class required for training. Our results on the classification of data from the 1D, 2D, and 3D domains demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in various complex and periodic data scenarios.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation rely solely on adapting features but fail to utilize cause features that remain unaffected by the shift, thus remaining unexploited. We propose a semi-generative model that adapts both effect and cause conditions while also leveraging cause features for generating data not present in the training set. From a theoretical perspective, we establish the minimum sample requirements for reliable estimation and demonstrate experimentally that plugging in non-parametric estimators achieves efficient sample utilization.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level.

We examine the connection between the principal factor analysis model and a combinatorial concept of minimum for vectors of integers within the positive definite lattice. Our investigation reveals that the principal factor model can be interpreted as finding such minima in embedded lattices, and the model's theoretical components, including its minimum solution and factor score, correspond to the lattice minimum and its projection, respectively. Furthermore, the examination of specific examples, including a case related to quantum gravity, demonstrates the model's effectiveness and efficiency, and its application extends to scoring items in situations with a variety of characteristics even if their nature is unknown. Our analysis also provides a theoretical justification that the principal factor analysis model produces superior results, including improved scores, when working within a lattice framework rather than traditional Euclidean space.

A research framework is introduced to uncover and analyze decision-making processes from deep neural network classifiers in jet substructure tagging techniques. To achieve this, the study uses a new set of variables designed by particle physicists as well as pre-trained activation features from a CNN tagger, and demonstrates that these variables can be effectively utilized without discarding any original inputs. By employing a layer-by-layer analysis, the study reveals that each neural network layer focuses on distinct sets of variables and ultimately interprets the outcomes in a manner similar to the decision-making process made by human physicists. Furthermore, analyzing the relevance of layers within high-performing feed-forward networks indicates that some deeper layers are highly relevant and should not be severed, in contrast to convolutional neural networks where very deep layers are less relevant.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties allowed for the efficient computation of relevant physical characteristics using symbolic methods, thanks to code such as POLSym. This involved an initial step of categorizing irreducible domains based on their action within the Brillouin zone and the topology of the torus. Additionally, band representations stemming from site symmetry groups were broken down into irreducible components. This theoretical data on layer group symmetry was then tabulated and made accessible online.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of the positon equation, where they are found to be expressed using Killing vector fields. These vector fields can generate symmetry transformations, which correspond to conservation laws in quantum systems. It turns out that the Killing vector fields corresponding to momentum operators in this context are specifically vector fields that generate isometries of the underlying manifold's metric. For system (1.1), the isometries happen to be movement symmetries of its confining potential. The general conditions for a Killing vector field to generate geodesic integral curves are discussed and it's demonstrated how the canonical commutation relations among these vector fields relate to structure constants of the corresponding Lie algebra.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

In a composite Higgs model, we introduce doublet flavons to restore naturalness, while also generating Yukawa terms that account for fermion masses through the broken symmetry. This model incorporates global $SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R$ and $U(1)_{B-L}$ as exact aspects of the constituent quarks' flavor, leading to the generation of a mass matrix that matches the 3-generation structure due to the different generation numbers of left- and right-handed quarks. As a result, this framework naturally explains the hierarchical patterns in the fermion sector, including fermion masses and mixing angles. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the model's parameters align well with experimental findings when the compositeness scale, denoted as $\Lambda$, is set at approximately 1 TeV.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, enhances the capabilities of modern VR. By altering the user's perception, they allow for extended interactions within virtual environments or simulate infinite spaces. Previous research has explored the manipulations' impacts on human locomotion and movement, yet the effect on users' motor behavior remains unexplored. We conducted an experiment utilizing a redirected walking VR to investigate the limitations imposed by manipulated sensory inputs on users' movement. Our study utilized the "small world" effect, a phenomenon where manipulated walls create the illusion of a compact environment. We observed the limitations on users' movement and found that when navigating unknown environments, manipulated environments can mislead users, undermining their navigation abilities. Furthermore, our research raises significant ethical concerns, posing the risk of causing harm in applications that deceive users' spatial navigation. Consequently, it is essential to reevaluate existing ethical guidelines and establish new standards for VR technologies that manipulate user senses.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details about the mass distribution in protostellar binary systems formed through core fragmentation. Our investigation focuses on the mass formation of binary systems resulting from a core's spontaneous formation, where two sub-cores emerge and subsequently decrease in density. Assuming a power-law mass distribution for a protostellar core, where a typical formation mass of 0.3 solar masses is observed, our results indicate that higher mass peaks correspond to significantly larger total masses. Specifically, our analysis reveals that as the mass parameter 'm' increases, the mass formed in binary systems rises, ultimately exceeding 100 solar masses when 'm' reaches 3.5. Our further examination into the effects of angular momentum, a crucial factor in binary system development, shows increased mass formation compared to scenarios without considering angular momentum effects, with the most substantial impact observed when 'm' reaches values of 1.5 to 1.7, resulting in up to two to four times greater mass than models accounting for angular momentum at lower 'm' values.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach for extracting relevant features from data sets with disparate scales. A new kernel function is developed based on the scaled hyperbolic arcsinh transformation. A simulation study was conducted to evaluate the performance of this approach. Both the theoretical and practical findings demonstrate that data scales can significantly impede the performance of FastICA, while a combination of a scalable kernel and a linear transformation offers an effective solution. Notably, a data set with skewed scales exhibited comparable accuracy to that of balanceded data using our proposed method. Overall, this study highlights the importance of both new transformation techniques and scalable kernel functions in feature extraction processes.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's proven that if a logic system can identify unique, non-isomorphic graphs using only its own language, then a corresponding polynomial degree calculation can also identify these properties. This calculation was adapted to the extended polynomial calculus, a system that can simulate SAT-solving tools like DPLL. Consequently, it was found that extended polynomial calculus cannot be efficiently simulated by DPLL, a long-standing theory. Furthermore, it was established that the BKLM reduction technique is inefficient due to its potential exponential growth in proof size. In the context of extended calculus, this paper shows that the Berman et al. reduction method is not universally applicable and a more direct approach is proposed.

A subring collection is $\sigma$-elementary if it has the $\sigma$-closure property: for any ring sharing a language with the subring, any extension of its elements in the ring's elements must be in the subring. We demonstrate an infinite family of subring collections that are $\sigma$-elementary, particularly those derived from ideal and quotient operations on principal ideal domains. Notably, a particular subring collection, defined by ideals and quotients on $\Z$, does not share this property.

Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their authenticity can be challenging due to their subjective nature. Our research aims to categorize unfalsifiable claims made on social media by剖析ing threads with substantial user engagement, and we've devised a framework to extract and explore the underlying structural elements. This framework enables us to extract multiple types of claims - such as those supported by consensus, with circular reasoning, acting as coping mechanisms, and incorporating metaphors. We also present these findings in context, including the connections established among user-generated content.

Identifying trending social media events in space and time is essential for its own merit, particularly in anticipating and responding to emerging events. The rapid growth of geotagged social media content makes it possible, but also extremely challenging, due to a massive amount of data. The task entails monitoring real-time updates and extracting valuable information from social media to pinpoint evolving events in real-time. An analysis of the phenomenon combines spatial and temporal elements, necessitating a careful balance between detection accuracy and computational efficiency. We present a novel event detection framework designed for real-time spatio-temporal social media events, focusing on balancing accuracy and false positives in streaming data. The framework utilizes a Bayesian filter to update the likelihood of events based on temporal information and a adaptive sampling algorithm that prioritizes relevant information based on expected accuracy gains. Our framework enables reliable real-time event detection, outperforming existing approaches both spatially and temporally while reducing computational load during temporal event tracking. The proposed system was tested using a major geolocation-based social media data set during the Tokyo Olympics and surpasses location-based event detection benchmarks by over 50%.

New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background and baryonic
large-scale structure observations will allow researchers to study the cross-correlation
of these datasets with the CMB lensing potential, leading to enhanced constraints on
primordial non-Gaussianity. The coefficient $f_{NL}$ of the primordial
non-Gaussianity can be studied by analyzing the CMB lensing potential's spectral density
landscape in the three-dimensional bispectrum space. This paper presents a fast method
called Skew, which computes the bispectrum by convolving the power spectra of the three
datasets using an efficient FFT-based algorithm. The accuracy and stability of Skew are
verified by comparing its results to full numerical evaluations of the bispectrum. The
results show that Skew significantly accelerates the estimation of the bispectrum's
amplitude amplitude. The approach will facilitate the analysis of the non-linear cosmic
structure's evolution.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10. Notably, our framework produced BNNs that were only marginally larger in size compared to their non-robust counterparts, while providing superior uncertainty estimation. This innovation sets the stage for future research into the development of BNNs that can be trained efficiently and used for adaptive testing against potential attacks.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020, with China being the initial country affected and managed to contain the virus effectively. In contrast, Europe and the United States struggled with inaction, leading to a delayed and disorganized response. This inaction fueled the proliferation of online rumors in their populations. As a result, an in-depth investigation of the pandemic-related rumor mill in these regions proves highly necessary. By collecting and analyzing a large dataset of WeChat moments content from China, we were able to gain a deeper understanding of the structural characteristics governing the dissemination of rumors. Furthermore, we developed a set of algorithms to accurately measure the level of personal credibility associated with the propagation of rumors. Our research revealed that certain types of rumors tend to propagate faster, with the personal credibility of the individual sharing the rumor playing a significant role in its dissemination. In summary, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving the spread of rumors during the pandemic in China, Europe and the United States.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness. A case study involving the Hyperspectral Image Spectrometers for terrestrial EXoplanet research (HI-SEXPEx) instrument is employed to evaluate spectral dimensionality reduction techniques. Additionally, this research outlines the steps for evaluating these techniques in dimensionality reduction and feature selection for planetary exoplanet research.

Neural networks are highly effective at solving complex problems, but they often require significant computational resources and energy due to large model sizes. Compressing deep learning models is a critical research area that aims to reduce their size without sacrificing performance, leading to more accessible and scalable deployments in real-world applications. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of existing model compression techniques for natural language processing, aiming to help readers better understand and apply these techniques in practice.

The positions of atoms in proteins are crucial as they determine the functional interactions within a molecule. Despite this, determining the structures of proteins can be challenging due to constraints limited by experimental data. Although various sources can provide valuable information on protein structures, none is sufficient on its own to accurately model the entire molecule. Therefore, supplementary information from existing data can help refine and validate the protein structure. This report presents a novel and efficient method that leverages high-throughput quantum mechanical calculations to guide the protein folding process. Our approach involves predicting the amide proton chemical shifts of proteins, which are then compared with experimental values. These predictions enable us to filter out unfavorable configurations, thereby expediting the protein folding process. The efficiency of our method is demonstrated by successfully predicting the structures of a protein and a peptide, which align closely with existing structures obtained through other means. Furthermore, our method validates these structures by comparing the calculated chemical shifts with experimental values. The results show a remarkable correlation, reflecting a strong agreement between our predictions and observed data.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key factor in its training process, yet its selection is often done randomly by researchers. This study examines the effect of ten diverse loss functions for classification on the performance of neural networks, focusing on how neural network architecture influences this outcome. Through comprehensive data, we provide clear guidance on suitable loss functions, highlighting the critical role of the architecture, especially in the case of quantum neural network models. Notably, our findings show that switching from conventional loss functions to variable losses can substantially improve the neural network's classification accuracy, particularly when replacing cross-entropy with the q-X divergence loss, which can achieve a 4% boost in accuracy and differential privacy performance. Moreover, our research indicates that this improved loss significantly mitigates overfitting and offers a higher degree of privacy protection. These findings are valid across a range of datasets, and our study includes detailed mathematical representations for loss functions to facilitate their practical application, making it a valuable resource for the examination of quantum neural models.

Describing the behaviors of complex systems composed of strongly interacting elements poses significant challenges due to an insurmountable number of interactions. Parquet theory, incorporating various types of correlations, offers a promising framework for understanding such systems, yet solving the associated equations remains a daunting task. We propose a novel Hamiltonian approach to streamline the calculation of the self-energy by applying Van der Waals' theorem, thus bypassing the need to directly solve the integral equations. Notably, this new method still relies on an approximation to achieve its goal, so its worth lies in offering a fresh avenue for developing more advanced approximations. Additionally, we demonstrate the compatibility of our formalism with self-consistent solutions and anticipate its potential to provide an alternative starting point for exploring Wigner's original ideas.

The purpose of this work was to employ quantum Monte Carlo to investigate exciton condensation in a 2D semiconductor, specifically in TiSe_2. To achieve this, our approach involved calculating dynamic properties using random phase approximation, incorporating corrections via exciton diffusion chain expansion, for the Fermi gas Hamiltonian. Employing a real-space approach bypassed the limitations of maraging steel, allowing us to accurately model the K point connectivity in the Brillouin zone. By fixing the carrier density, our method involved locating the ground state wavefunction via exciton diffusion Monte Carlo, grounding our results in rigorously known wavefunctions. Consequently, our calculations revealed an onset of exciton condensation below the experimental transition temperature in TiSe_2. Moreover, our work substantiated that the 2D wavefunction exhibited significant momentum resolution, conforming to recent findings from angstrom-x-ray photoemission spectroscopy. Additionally, our results aligned with ultrafast transmission electron microscopy, demonstrating that the exciton phase transition did not cause bandgaps in MoSe_2 to shift.

In the US, text-based systems allowed individuals to report safety issues like vandalism and drug problems, especially in the 1980s and 1990s. These systems evolved into modern digital platforms that continue to support community members in communicating with local authorities about various safety concerns. While effective in facilitating communication, a significant number of interactions described in these platforms are difficult to interpret with existing data due to ambiguous language and missing context. This study examines a large dataset of user-submitted safety concerns paired with dispatcher instructions, revealing challenges in automatically understanding community safety conversations. These challenges stem from issues like implicit information, complex sent structures, ambiguous language, and non-standard terminology. To address these difficulties, this study proposes advanced data cleaning methods, natural language understanding techniques, and human expertise in curating a dataset that can be used to automatically discover factual information and the process of reasoning required to filter out irrelevant context. Additionally, this study highlights the inherent complexity and challenging nature of social safety issues and their interactions.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and conventional singlet superconductors using the mean-field model. Although superconductors are generally immune to magnetic fields, triplet s-wave superconductors in a triplet state can be magnetized. Conversely, triplet p-wave superconductors with nematic ground states are expected to have a decreased magnetic susceptibility when in the superconducting state compared to their normal state counterparts.

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, unlabelled data points to obtain annotations, focusing on improving model performance with minimal labels. However, current active learning methods are limited by their inability to handle uncertainty. We propose a new minimax active learning approach that addresses this shortcoming by employing a two-player game framework to develop strategies for minimizing loss and maximizing uncertainty simultaneously. Our Minimax Active Learning (MAL) algorithm builds upon the inverse dynamics of a two-player game to find optimal strategies that minimize the distance between model predictions and actual labels, while maximising prediction uncertainty. In a step-wise training process, MAL continues training as long as there is uncertainty, demonstrating significant improvements over existing methods on various benchmark datasets, including Cifar10 and MNIST.

To study how music changed over time from the year 1960 to 2010, we measured the
variety of songs in the Million Song Dataset using several elements, including
melodic structure, melodic variety, and rhythm. Each song was represented as a
sequence of notes and durations. We identified the most prevalent song types
from each decade, termed typical songs, which reflect both typical songs of that
time and those that underwent significant style shifts. We found that typical
songs display characteristics typical of Western music in each respective decade,
and when compared within each decade, they exhibited lower entropy in melody,
higher structure in rhythm, and increased complexity in chords. Additionally, we
determined that songs adapting to new styles often experienced a substantial
decrease in chord complexity.

A novel category of stochastic processes that integrate reinforcement mechanisms is presented, featuring multiple entries and governed by independent integers. Based on this class, two specific models are developed: one utilizing uniform distribution and the other incorporating Beta-distribution for additional reinforcement. Capitalizing on existing proof techniques, we derive several key findings that are specific to these models that are similar in nature to existing proofs. Utilizing this class of models with uniform distribution, we establish a strong law of large numbers, a central limit theorem, and a characterization for the convergence of the processes to Non-Homogeneous Stick-Breaking processes through the application of the previous two theorems. Furthermore, when this class of models with additional reinforcement governed by Beta-distributions is employed, we establish a central limit theorem for both models that are based on variance-stabilizing transformations and direct analysis, respectively.

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms on the real plane vanishing at infinity. The results show that a specific subgroup within these diffeomorphisms preserves the shape and configuration of the vortex loops, making them visible. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence of periodic motion in this configuration space, indicating the possibility of changing the relative positions of the vortex loops over time in a predictable manner.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome to incorporate potential confounders, then applying predictions to the outcome model for different treatment levels with ATE equal to the difference in predictions between the two extremes.  Three studies have emphasized the importance of the second step, utilizing neural networks for optimal nonparametric modeling and outcomes similar to ATE.  A new method presented here shifts focus to the first step, which often utilizes simpler models, and incorporates an influential covariate adjustment using the inverse probability weighting technique.  This approach incorporates neural network estimations of the treatment probability and incorporates neural network estimations of the treatment and outcome using data exclusively from out-of-support cases.  Simulation results indicate that this approach yields better outcomes than existing two-step methods.

The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current research into lepton flavor universality violations in B-physics, warranting greater theoretical attention in the coming years. Enhanced data samples from Belle-II, as well as LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS, will be crucial in further investigating this area. Additionally, insights from $\tau$ decays into pions will be relevant to the puzzles in B-meson physics. Consequently, this has led to a resurgence in the study of $\tau$ physics within the context of the Standard Model and beyond, driven by both experimental and theoretical motivations. A key focus here includes utilizing the precise measurements of $\tau$ polarization and decay properties to pinpoint the weak and electromagnetic form factors of the one-pion state, as well as two-pion and lepton states, enabling a direct comparison between experimental data and theoretical predictions based on lattice QCD and other methods. Ultimately, this effort aims to test the Standard Model's limits, with special emphasis on new-physics effects in two-pion states, three-pion states, and four-lepton states in $\tau$ decays.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied over the years as a laboratory model for atmospheric cyclogenesis, where experiments have been meticulously documented. Recently, numerical simulations using a simplified model have been conducted using the OpenFOAM framework, revealing strong agreement with the experimental findings in terms of momentum and heat transfer. This study presents a comprehensive comparison of the experimental data with the open-source numerical model using various benchmarks, showcasing high consistency between the two. As a result, the numerical simulation demonstrates its reliability and can be used as an effective tool for studying and understanding the dynamics of cyclogenesis, particularly in predicting heights of pressure at specific time intervals.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences that exceed an unusually high threshold as events following a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this approach has significant implications, its effectiveness is hindered due to the lack of available parametric distribution forms, especially when trying to accurately model the intricate pattern parameter variation. This study presents a novel mathematical representation for the intensity function, enabling precise flexibility in two out of three parameters, and provides control for the pattern parameter as the threshold increases. Furthermore, it introduces a method for estimating all parameters via maximum likelihood estimation, and validates its performance through simulations. Ultimately, the methodology is applied to analyse the incidence of intense daily rainfall in Chongqing, China.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, a significant issue arises when a dataset used for training is contaminated by examples that were not involved in the original data collection. This problem significantly hinders the development of policies that can be generalized from the corrupted dataset. Current offline RL methods primarily rely on assuming a certain level of contamination, which limits their effectiveness. This paper explores the development of more robust offline RL algorithms that can adapt to varying levels of contamination rates. The proposed algorithms not only guarantee statistical efficiency but also achieve an optimal complexity of O(1/ε²) in terms of dependency on the desired accuracy. Additionally, this paper introduces a variant of the Variance Reduced Proximal Policy Optimization (PROX-Policy Mirror Descent) that can efficiently handle data with unequal sampling distributions. The robust and generalization-capable algorithms developed in this paper are tested in two settings: the classic gridworld environment and the more complex Robox-tower setting, demonstrating their potential for practical applications.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison.

In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like the biological motors, they also help convert electron energy into mechanical motion. A key innovation was combining single-molecule fluorescence with electrical measurements, which enabled direct observation of the mechanical movement of the motors. This approach provides further support for studying artificial molecular motors through various models like Brownian machines, and our research specifically focuses on developing a basic dynamic model for these motors powered by inelastic electron tunneling and presents potential directions for future theoretical and experimental studies.

Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of determining whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way model, with a limit to how complex this transformation can be. Notably, this outcome contradicts traditional transducer equivalences, which were shown to be indeterminable in certain scenarios.

This article investigates the concept of generalizing convolutions. We start by defining a generalized convolution as a quadrilinear map from four vector spaces. Then, we examine its direct computational method and indirect computation through Fast Fourier Transform. By comparing the costs of these methods, we find that the FFT-based approach outperforms the direct method under a wide range of conditions. To illustrate our findings, we consider two specific cases: bicommutative algebras and unital algebras.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial evidence that brown dwarfs could exist beyond the mass limitations of stars, but its complex atmospheric composition has remained unclear for over two decades. Recent observations by the Keck telescope between 2013 and 2019 provided high-quality spectra (S/N ~ 100) across 1-2.4 micrometers, enabling a thorough re-evaluation of its atmospheric composition. By employing an advanced retrieval analysis with the APOLLO code and rigorous MARMOT modeling, a detailed characterization of GJ 229B was achieved. Our findings, remarkably precise, revealed a temperature of 639 (+8, -6) K and chemical abundances consistent with solar ratios for C/O and metallicity [M/H], with individual element variations of +/- 0.25 dex for CO2, +/- 0.20 dex for H2O, and similar precision for other gases. Moreover, our advanced modeling, uncommon for such early-type T-dwarves, accounted for non-grey opacity and cloud effects. Although some model uncertainties persist, particularly the cloud opacity, our advanced modeling and individual line-by-line retrieval for specific molecular bands yielded consistent results. Our advanced modeling and individual line-by-line retrieval for specific molecular bands yielded consistent results.

To search for the potential existence of the unique $0^{--}$ state, we created a systematic approach to designing tetraquark operators. In the process, we found that $0^{+-}$ tetraquark operators have previously been identified. Utilizing the technique we developed, the correlation functions for both $0^{--}$ and $0^{+-}$ operators were computed, and their spectrum under different spin configurations of quark pairs was subject to detailed analysis, resulting in key insights. Our findings indicate that the $0^{--}$ operators exhibit significantly weaker coupling compared to $0^{+-}$ operators, and we argue that this suggests the absence of $0^{--}$ hadronic states. In a contrast, multiple evidence points to strong coupling and multiple potential states for $0^{+-}$ operators.

A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to establish the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ caused by $\bar{b}\to\bar{c}c\bar{s}$ decays. The precise prediction of $\phi_{s}$ within the Standard Model makes it a favorable means for detecting signs of new physics. The experiment's $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ measurements are discussed in detail.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant in any confined setting where humans are gathered.

This study has conducted large-scale shell-model computations for $\beta$-decay attributes. Researchers at ILL, Grenoble, recently performed $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy to investigate $\beta$-decay properties related to the transition of $^{137}$Te ($7/2^-$) into $^{137}$I with an experimentally unknown spin and parity. By doing so, they discovered for the first time, a two-proton forbidden $\beta$-decay from an odd-numbered neutron. Our calculations determined a 95% probability that $^{137}$I is indeed $6^+$ and found a 2.5% $\beta$-decay branching ratio for $^{137}$Te to $^{137}$I. Furthermore, we computed several key shell-model parameters for both the $\beta$-decay of $^{135}$Te and for single-nucleon matrix elements. Our findings have contributed substantially to understanding the $\beta$-decay process in this particular region.

Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single dimension of product features. To address the limitation, we developed an approach that accounts for multiple dimensions, resulting in either partial trades across various dimensions or complete trades in all dimensions. This approach also resulted in significant verification of the algorithm. Notably, we discovered that the new method makes a service more valuable to customers by optimizing trade-offs across different dimensions of the service.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we assessed their physical feasibility and concluded that the decay widths are extremely narrow. The results further enabled us to estimate the lifetime of these mesons.

Michal Szabados initially proposed a theory in his doctoral dissertation. In this current paper, the proposed conjecture is examined by the authors, specifically a Ph.D. hypothesis by Michal Szabados. Initially, the researchers demonstrate that an evaluation could be narrowed down to a periodic structure, defined over a specific and limited character set. It is further established that Szabados's conjecture is true for a considerable class of non-regular patterns. This includes all low-convex patterns of relatively simple complexity.

In modern research, reduced-order models are often developed using dimensionality reduction methods like Proper Orthogonal Decomposition to analyze and predict complex phenomena in various fields, including fluid mechanics, pattern recognition, and optimization. Utilizing kernel techniques for a more efficient dimensionality reduction has emerged as a promising approach for optimizing computational efficiency. However, current methods face significant challenges due to the limited ability of traditional linear models to capture intricate patterns. The inclusion of higher-order statistical moments in dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) can yield better results, especially for linear and nonlinear problems. Introducing a new variational framework that employs kernel learning for LANDO, we offer a with-nuclei optimization method that efficiently handles the computation of higher-order moments through optimally placed data sampling points. This novel approach enables the accurate reconstruction of higher-order moments as vector-valued functions in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space, thus simplifying the computation and overcoming the "curse of dimensionality." Numerical experiments confirm that our method produces accurate dynamic modes and spectra and are applicable to various linear and nonlinear problems, regardless of the dimensionality of data. This research provides a link between kernel techniques and reduced-order modeling, opening new avenues for machine learning in scientific computing.

The timeless appeal of chess persists, with its intricacies and beauty continuing to captivate players today. Our focus lies in analyzing the chess openings employed by contemporary players, both live and on virtual platforms. Our analysis draws from the GitHub repository of 'Chess Opening Collection'. By examining the frequencies of various openings, both statistically and visually, we provide insights into the most and least common 'families' of openings. Furthermore, we introduce a visual representation method, utilizing heat maps and numerical analysis, to assess the complexity and similarity of these structures. Our research also considers the impact of 'difficulty coefficients' on players and their chosen openings, providing a refined perspective on the subject. Ultimately, our findings, including heat maps and numerical assessments, can aid experts and enthusiasts in comprehending contemporary opening preferences and their frequency.

This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse.

A method to derive constants of motion beyond local bounds for ODE-based Lagrangian systems is outlined, including a practical example that illustrates its utility for dissipative mechanical systems and its implications on solution existence and behavior under specific assumptions. The framework is further extended to cover Euler-Lagrange equations with order greater than two, yielding new first integrals for particular models, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, paving the way for potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future.

Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Nonetheless, the field remains limited by the low-quality inputs and high effort involved in using 2D image-based queries. To overcome these limitations, this research explores the use of rough 3D sketches as query inputs for 3D retrieval tasks, specifically in the context of the ModelNet10 dataset. The proposed method involves converting raw Open3D sketch inputs into a format suitable for neural processing through the application of deep learning. A synthetic, detailed mesh with accompanying images is then generated using a convolutional neural network, and finally compared with database images through visual similarity to identify matching shapes. The results indicate that this method successfully demonstrates the feasibility of rough 3D sketches as effective queries for 3D retrieval tasks.

HD 80606 b is a unique planet with characteristics of a gas giant, resembling the Jupiter we know, yet it has an unusual 1-month orbit around its host star, characterized by significant variations in stellar brightness and radiation it experiences.  Its short afternoon followed by a long night it experiences on its surface create extreme conditions that gas giant's atmospheric and climate systems might undergo, making it an exciting target for studying the atmospheric and radiation properties of eccentric giant planets that future space telescopes like the powerful James Webb Space Telescope can explore.  In order to take full advantage of these opportunities, it is essential for researchers to have an accurate and reliable understanding of the planet's orbit, particularly its specific timing it passes close to its host star, referred to as its periastron.  This article provides an in-depth analysis and comparison of the current and proposed models that predict this periastron passage with remarkable precision, revealing an intriguing potential shift in the orbit's timing it foretells to occur every other year.  Utilizing long-term observational data it possesses and the powerful VLTI telescope, researchers have been able to make significant progress in accurately predicting the orbit's timing it possesses, leading to an essential step in classifying it with high confidence.  This accurate prediction will ensure that researchers can schedule their observations of the planet with ease and efficiency it deserves.

In this investigation, we're looking at how a specific type of matter collapse, governed by a certain relationship between pressure and density, behaves according to the general theory of relativity. The effect of this relationship on the mass of the collapsing matter is explored. The analysis reveals that for this type of matter behavior, both increase and decrease in mass during collapse are possible. Since one scenario requires pressure to increase with density, while the other requires an opposite trend, it's concluded that these two outcomes represent fundamentally different physical processes and thus can't be uniformly applied in solving the general relativity equations.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a systematic approach for calculating corrections to extremal black holes. This method clarifies the underlying reasons for discrepancies between various techniques. Furthermore, the framework enables the efficient management of intricate expressions that typically complicate traditional methods. Using this framework, we have successfully computed the first and second-order charge contributions to the extremal Kerr-Newman black hole's entropy. Our results show that these corrections are purely charge-dependent and that the corrections to the entropy match those from previous studies that assumed charge contributions were extremal.

A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome distribution, which can be achieved by optimizing a driving force that keeps system trajectories within high-probability regions of the target distribution. Previous studies utilized a dual-control framework for end-effector-driven systems, combining a traditional trajectory planner with a 1-to-1 mapping explorer. Our approach reimagines this concept by utilizing a more flexible multi-to-many exploration strategy that seeks to match a desired outcome distribution. This research delves into the underlying principles of this planner, presenting a systematic exploration drive method that gradually refines a basic probabilistic model into a more complex structure capable of effectively bridging the gap between current and target distributions. Our algorithm demonstrates strong performance in a variety of complex movement generation and learning applications, effectively inverting a wide array of outcome distributions for both robotic and biological motion.

A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring generalised models of massive and massless free particles in three dimensions. Multiple generalised particle models have been presented, which distinguish themselves in terms of the coloured Poincaré orbits they describe. Our methodology provides a potential pathway to describing particles in non-abelian backgrounds and serves as a starting point for the worldline formulation of an associated quantum field theory.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs and outerplanar graphs.

Image-based goal navigation is a common approach in autonomous systems, allowing a agent to choose the next action by comparing a pre-defined goal image with the current observation. Recent advancements in learning from simulation-to-real transfer have relied on storing an extensive number of past experiences (memories) to determine the most suitable action at each step. However, storing all past simulations leads to memory saturation and performance degradation. Our proposed method, MemoNav, employs a novel attention-based architecture to selectively choose relevant memories for training, effectively balancing global memory access and current situation awareness. By training with only a small subset of selected memories, MemoNav significantly reduces the computational load compared to full-access performance, achieving nearly identical results with negligible degradation. As a result, MemoNav not only enhances training efficiency but also allows for a larger memory size without detrimental performance effects. Our findings indicate superior performance compared to the baseline method in navigation tasks, particularly when the agent encounters unfamiliar real-world environments. Moreover, MemoNav's performance remains robust even after sim-to-real transfer.

To increase cellular capacity, implement enhanced network functionalities and accommodate a vast array of diverse applications, small cells have been widely adopted in the NR-5G standard, supporting diverse in-band and out-of-band deployment methods including subterranean, urban, rural, and sea-based environments. Despite their advantages, the deployment of small cells poses a challenge: it requires optimizing a vast array of variables to achieve the ideal configuration, rendering traditional solution methods inefficient. Consequently, this paper provides a thorough analysis, beginning with an introduction to small cells followed by an examination of various RAN architectures, small cell deployment strategies and backhaul networking frameworks associated with 4G and 5G 400GHz frequency bands. Furthermore, it encompasses an overview of pivotal aspects such as resource allocation, backhaul routing, small cell placement, network configuration, equipment setup, operational procedures and standard protocols, assuming diverse user distributions and requirements, thereby facilitating the optimal small cell deployment, thereby improving the overall network efficiency. Finally, the anticipated innovations in small cell technology expected to be integrated into 6G standard are also highlighted.

We've developed a comprehensive framework to model complex interactions between multiple entangled systems using hypergraphs. This approach can be applied to several processes and we'll specifically explore how certain conditions lead to spontaneous pattern emergence in systems where individual units interact with each other. Our focus will be on two specific settings: one involving interactions between groups over long distances, and another with diffusive interactions between units. Additionally, we'll demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through applications to both the generalized Volterra system and the Brusselator model.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to investigate operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner. Our research highlights the significance of eigenstate thermalization in operator behavior and reveals that it can be entanglement-driven in specific scenarios. Moreover, utilizing capacity concepts enables us to quantify operator complexity and its underlying structure effectively.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a highly excited state in carbon-12 composed of three clusters of alpha particles, is a subject of interest in terms of how it decomposes into an excited state of boron-11 and a proton or a ground-state of beryllium-11 and an alpha particle. Theoretical predictions by various models are at variance, so researchers conducted an experiment using the J-PARC G-2M experiment to study this decay process and find that the majority of the reaction resulted in the formation of the boron-11 excited state and a proton, which supports a common theoretical model. However, researchers found that the boundary between the two reaction outcomes was less distinct than expected and used machine learning to identify the boundary, resulting in a calculated value of 2.4 MeV for the boundary, which is a relatively high value. Although this calculation is limited by a lack of data at lower energies, it is believed to be a reasonable upper limit.

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture dynamics have been made in recent years. The observations of highly oscillating crack patterns are not new. Recent experiments have highlighted their appearance at low crack speeds when the intrinsic material length scale is considered. To gain a deeper understanding of oscillatory and tip-splitting instabilities in a simple brittle material model that accounts for material length and time scales, we conducted a comprehensive study. These theoretical and numerical investigations have shown that an instability diagram can be established when the time scale is fixed, offering valuable insights into the factors governing these instabilities.

In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels equipped with feedback and state information, which becomes available to the encoder in a predictable sequence. This encompasses a broad range of channels, including memoryless channels with independent and identically distributed states (referred to as the Shannon strategy), channels with Markovian states that offer the ability to access past states (known as look-ahead access) and energy harvesting. The capacity of these channels with feedback is described in terms of the directed information between auxiliary variables and the channel outputs. Additionally, we provide specific results on the existence of finite length codes that can achieve the described capacities, taking into consideration the availability of look-ahead access. Moreover, we establish a direct relationship between these findings and control theory, specifically in the context of a common stochastic control problem, the separation principle, which shows that under certain conditions, the encoding can be achieved through a specific encoder structure that involves data compression and directed information rates. This leads to the knowledge of the directed I-D decomposition, which has been applied in various settings such as channels with look-ahead access and controlled harvesting.

A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a magnetic field may exhibit a unique and exceptionally robust type of superconductivity known as topological superconductivity. Employing an interaction-based approach based on the Rashba model with attractive forces, we demonstrate the emergence of topological superconductivity through the application of strong spin-orbit coupling, an optimized magnetic field setting, and in a two-dimensional system. Our findings reveal that the threshold for this topological superconductivity occurs at lower values of these parameters when applied two-dimensionally as opposed to three-dimensionally. Utilizing the Cooper pair wave function, we examine the behavior of surface states that feature Miyazaki states on the system's surface areas, presenting a counter-intuitive phenomenon on the reverse of spin-orbit coupling.

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize both the structure and content of tabular data to make informed decisions and draw conclusions in various domains such as finance and real estate. This research project aimed to address this challenge by developing a dataset and corresponding BERT-based models to assist in the verification of factual information contained within tables. Contributing to the OpenReview SEMEval 2021 platform, this project provides the anticipated dataset and model resources to support the related task.

This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

We have developed a set of nonlinear partial differential equations that account for ground water's interaction with the atmosphere in regions outside of conventional local drainage zones. These equations take into consideration the thin-film flow dynamics that occur in the porous ground. The problem was initially simplified in[1] using the Reynolds equation, which however did not adequately capture the ultra-slow movements of water in the atmosphere. Our model incorporates two additional processes: (1) the formation of "micro-cavities" in the atmosphere when water levels drop and (1) the continuation of atmospheric drainage from high-density areas to low-density areas even when "caustics" are present. As a result, the nonlinear equations are more accurate in modeling the movement of water in the atmosphere. The problem also involves solving for the "caustic" evolution over time. We have established the existence and uniqueness of solutions in a limited time period. The model's complexity makes it difficult to verify global existence. Several simplified models are compared, including one that models the "caustic" as impermeable and another that doesn't. The latter is implemented in a computer code. The model's ability to predict water table evolution is also tested.

This work has investigated the potential of advanced oxidation processes using ultraviolet radiation and ozone to transform nitrogen dioxide in flue gas. Additionally, the removal of NO is also examined. We conducted numerical simulations in a laboratory-scale vertical flow reactor with a 14 W UV lamp, feeding it a mixed gas of nitrogen, oxygen, NO, and $H_2O$. The study found that UV radiation alone is insufficient for effective removal of NOx, but adding ozone significantly enhances O$_3$-based removal of both NO and nitrogen dioxide. We found that a specific ratio of ozone to nitrogen dioxide is optimal for minimizing ozone consumption, and that no such ratio exists for the oxidation of NO. The study found that most NO is converted to $NO_2$ but remains trapped in the form of ozone.

Emulating neuromorphic architectures at speed is crucial to evaluating their performance. The current industry standard, HSCLP, falls short in achieving speed for diverse neuromorphic models due to sequential processing and simulation delays. Our proposed solution involves integrating HSCL with SystemC MT for parallel simulation, utilizing the VLIW architecture's inherent capabilities to simulate multiple models concurrently and thus reduce overall emulation time.

In many real-world scenarios, AI systems face challenges when predicting outcomes due to uncertainties that can be clearly quantified. The nature of uncertainties can also be complex, such as when they cannot be precisely measured, and require complex representations that defy standard statistical methods.  tree models have shown great potential in handling这种情况 by using quantification to represent uncertainties as probabilities of different outcomes, but they struggle when uncertainties are multi-dimensional, and their difficulty increases exponentially.

This study presents a novel approach to tackle the challenges of reasoning under quantified uncertainties through the use of decision trees that can handle logical uncertainties as opposed to probabilistic uncertainties. These decision trees are efficient in handling multi-dimensional uncertainties through argument-based reasoning that draws on rules with conditions that can be logically evaluated. The results indicate that the new decision tree model rivals state-of-the-art methods in their accuracy for scenarios with clear uncertainties, but excels in scenarios where uncertainties cannot be precisely measured.

The DTW distance is frequently applied in time series analysis across various fields, but its computational efficiency is a significant drawback, especially for similarity-search applications. To address this issue, some strategies have been employed to accelerate DTW computations, such as Lower Bound Distance, which facilitates early termination of unnecessary operations. Notably, the LB distance can provide an exact DTW distance if all points fall within a specified margin of error, denoted as eps, of the DTW distance. In this research, an improved LB distance variant is developed that enables premature cessation of DTW calculations when it is evident that further point comparisons won't influence the final outcome, even if the LB distance exceeds the eps margin. This revised approach is termed LBdtw-EAB. To demonstrate its efficacy, the LBdtw-EAB is integrated into the DBSCAN clustering algorithm and a customized DTW-Index, which indexes time series data, for the purposes of efficient density-based anomaly detection and high-dimensional time series similarity search. Experimental findings indicate that LBdtw-EAB outperforms existing LB distance variants, yielding substantial speed improvements without compromising accuracy.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it lacks the ability to guide students towards more effective testing approaches. Some research has explored the ability to give constructive feedback, influencing students to create more coverage-oriented test cases, but the feedback, provided automatically, may feel patronizing to students. In this study, we propose an inquiry-based method to give feedback on testing shortcomings, requiring students to engage with concepts and apply them when analyzing their code's test coverage issues. A controlled experiment involving 128 sophomore students in a Java testing course was conducted to compare the effects of this inquiry-based method with more traditional feedback methods. Our findings show that the inquiry-based method has a greater positive impact on students' test case quality and overall learning outcomes, surpassing both the ability of automatic tools and human graders to provide meaningful feedback.

In domains requiring explanations from AI systems, it's particularly vital for these explanations to assist humans in understanding why specific decisions were made, not just by pinpointing relevant factors but also by clarifying their relative importance. Current approaches using independent and identically distributed data, however, often result in inconsistent local explanations that fail to provide such a comprehensive understanding. This study presents a novel concept analysis-based method, utilizing a question-answer pair framework, in which answerable questions represent the training samples, to generate global explanations that seamlessly integrate with human knowledge. We demonstrate through concept learning from incomplete and noisy data that this concept analysis approach yields more precise and conceptually clear interpretations, which we verify by comparing its results to those from an attention-based baseline on several tasks. Furthermore, the nature of the findings reflects the underlying knowledge within the data. Finally, we treat concept learning and explanations as a logic programming task, introducing a formalism based on literal and compound concepts and presenting an algorithm that uses iterative model refinement and the introduction of new concepts. This is accomplished by formulating concept inquiries and responses as logic programming rules. We verify the equivalence between the question-answer framework and our logic programming formulation on two tasks and show that the understanding and explanations generated are compatible with human knowledge.

Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon and Graph Convolutional Networks is presented in this article, including an estimation of the upper limit for its occurrence. The study sheds light on the pivotal elements contributing to over-smoothing and offers empirical evidence validating various countermeasures to mitigate it.

Dark matter production accompanying a leptonically decaying Z boson is investigated using Z boson signals derived from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. The experiment utilizes a dataset collected by the CMS detector at the LHC, totaling a 137 fb^-1 collision cross-section. To infer dark matter existence, anomalies are sought in collision outcomes featuring visible Z boson characteristics and unmeasurable transverse momentum. For direct comparison with dark matter particle interaction theories, simulated data are created assuming the mediators are scalar or vector particles and decay into a pair of dark matter particles and a Z boson. With this framework, the maximum permissible interaction cross-section is determined at various dark matter particle mass levels, ranging from 1 GeV to 10 GeV. At 25 GeV dark matter particle mass, the experiment's detection limits correspond to scalar mediator production crossings comparable to those of a multi-Petabecquerel electron beam collider, while vector mediator productions are broadly explored across mass differences of up to 13 TeV between the collider energy and the mediator mass.

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators.

Homeomorphisms with compact support on a Tychonoff space can be given several equivalent topological structures by viewing them as either a union of groups of homeomorphisms with bounded image support or as a subset of the group of all homeomorphisms of the space.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the growth of high-performance materials and facilitating the development of complex multilayer systems. Nevertheless, understanding and controlling the process remains a significant challenge. In a study on the growth of Heusler films on a graphene/sapphire substrate, it was discovered that when incorporating a specific element, In, in a Ca2IrO4 template, remote epitaxial growth occurred. Conversely, remote epitaxy was precluded by replacing In with a 5d element. Further research revealed that In's 5f electrons were responsible, due to their strong spin-orbit coupling interacting with graphene's piezoelectric ripples. Crucially, it was found that growth could be shifted from a remote to a van der Waals mechanism by increasing the cauldron height, indicating that controlling ripple-induced strain may enable effective remote epitaxy, even when this mechanism is currently outcompeted by van der Waals growth.

We analyze how to make predictions based on multivariate time series data that has extreme values and changing patterns. Traditional methods rely on assuming data follows a specific pattern, which we cannot rely on due to significant shifts such as those seen before major historical events. Recent breakthroughs have allowed researchers to analyze data with specific statistical characteristics, but this usually applies only to unchanging patterns. This study tackles the challenge of making predictions based on non-stationary time series with limited data and shows how patterns emerge over time with characteristics similar to long memory effects. It proposes using analysis based on patterns that can apply to various types of models and highlights the importance of considering changing patterns when making predictions.

Recent JWST observations of El Gordo (ACT-CL J0102-4915), the second most massive galaxy cluster found to date, yielded significant findings. They included the identification of multiple lensed arcs and redshifted objects spanning from hot gas down to distant galaxies. To analyze this unique system, we utilized the J-WARP algorithm on seven different JWST bands, uncovering 11 individual images of a highly lensed galaxy at the central region. With these data, we updated the convergence map and shear parameters compared to previous measurements. Furthermore, we found a newly lensed red supergiant star situated beyond the cluster. Located in the outer region, this object exhibited no significant consumption by the galaxy, likely due to suppressed star formation. It represents the farthest red superg giant discovered so far and the first of its kind in a galaxy cluster found by JWST. Our study also revealed a highly lensed galaxy at the central region of El Gordo with varying morphologies. Based on our analysis of the different shapes of the images, we found that the central galaxy has a complex structure, likely consisting of a spiral shape. This is supported by the symmetry of some of the images, which could not be fully explained by current lens models. Our study also highlighted a notable quenching of the central galaxy, likely due to the impact of the galaxy's merger history. With El Gordo, we are able to see into the galaxy formation and cluster

Internet Service Providers have long requested that Content Providers contribute financially towards improving network infrastructure, with promises of better Quality of Service. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the goal of mutual benefit. We model these negotiations through a simultaneous game in which Content Providers and Internet Service Providers decide on their levels of investment and revenue splitting proportions, respectively, in a two-stage process. We content provider's perspective, a type of game known as a Best Response Function, reveals that these agreements tend to exceed mutually advantageous outcomes. Conversely, by considering service provider responses, the situation resembles a version of the Dollar Auction game, a scenario in which all parties rarely achieve optimal results; in some instances, CPs refrain from participating in profit-sharing altogether, leading to lower overall investments compared to scenarios without these agreements.
