Building on prior work, we provide a rigorous foundation for existence and demonstrate uniqueness under specific conditions. This work builds on our investigation into weak measure-valued flows in higher dimensions.

Cybersecurity is crucial for devices with limited resources, and the challenge lies in classifying potential threats due to issues with conventional methods, such as their computational demands and inaccurate error rates. This paper presents a novel attack detection system that utilizes time-series data and a two-stage encoder, followed by Naive Bayes classification, to effectively recognize attack patterns in real-time on devices with restricted resources and classify network protocols. By utilizing readily available network traffic data and simple label markings, this model can be easily trained to achieve significant improvements, yielding an impressive 84% accuracy during real-world testing. Moreover, the encoder enables the system to adapt to new learning, and the model demonstrates a notable improvement, gaining at least 8% accuracy. By leveraging only time-series data, this approach simplifies training, and the NB classifier offers a gain, gaining at least 8% accuracy. By leveraging available labels, this system acquires an understanding of potential attack patterns, and the NB model demonstrates an impressive 84% accuracy during real-world testing, while the network attack classifier offers an advantage, yielding an impressive 84% accuracy during real-world testing.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this work is on the growth properties of semidirect products Hrtimes G, where H is the forfurther part of an arbitrary solvable group. More specifically, we investigate growth properties of actions of solvable groups. Our key finding is that in a solvable group G, a random permutation has finite orbit size if and only if it stabilizes a finite number of elements. Additionally, in certain cases such as polycyclic groups or finite extensions of abelian groups, we find a stronger condition where every orbit is finite. We also examine the-spectrum growth properties of-Growth and H, and establish specific criteria for its existence. Our work has specific applications to the group of units in upper triangular matrix rings over a finite field.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, escaping or pursuing, which they do by utilizing various forms of locomotion like locomotion on land, flying or swimming. By understanding how different biological entities move, we can gain valuable insights into their behavior and interactions with their surroundings. This paper proposes a computational approach to identify when a biological entity is moving and what form of locomotion it uses, by using only a video and the species' information. This is achieved by training two deep neural networks, one of which predicts motion and the other classifies locomotion methods. In initial testing on synthetic data, the network demonstrated high accuracy in identifying moments of movement, while a separate network trained on real-world data showed the ability to recognize when movement was caused by an object rather than self-locomotion. Finally, the proposed framework was successfully applied to video footage of swimming fish.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves challenging due to inherent measurement discrepancies that cause data to deviate from the underlying physical system. To address this issue, several frameworks have been proposed to separate measurement noise from true physical behavior. Despite these attempts, developing an accurate and stable model remains difficult due to multiple variables. Furthermore, incorporating constraints such as continuity and differentiability often necessitates complex mathematical formulations. In an effort to answer these questions, this thesis presents continuous and differentiable ML methods for automatic discovery of universal physical laws and corresponding models from data. In Chapter 1, two AI methods, i.e., continuous and differentiable optimization techniques, for determining universal physical laws and measurements are introduced to handle universal physical equations and measurements respectively. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the proposed AI methods are evaluated using three different mathematical models. In Chapter 2, an intelligent system for automatic discovery of universal physical equations and measurements is presented, which employs the ideas introduced in Chapter 1. In Chapter 3, an intelligent system for automatic discovery of universal physical equations and measurements is presented, which employs differentiability and a search-based method to determine universal physical equations and measurements. Finally, in Chapter 4, the successful application of the proposed AI methods in solving three different mathematical and physical problems is demonstrated, along with the discussion of their potential future developments and applications

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower speeds than light and distinctive characteristics: substantial transverse momentum and unusually large energy loss per unit length. The study focuses on a broad range of particle properties: those with masses up to 2500 GeV and particle energy loss capacities as low as 20 percent of the speed of light squared, across three distinct decay modes: completely stable particles, those decaying into a pair of super-light, stable particles, and those undergoing a delayed decay into a track and radiation emission. The study reveals no significant discrepancies from expected standard model behavior and establishes strict limitations on the existence of these particles in the context of various theoretical frameworks such as supersymmetry, $R$-parity even/odd models, and other theories involving $Z'$ and $Higgs$ portal interactions, long-lived particle decays of a $U(1)_{B-L}$ theory, and models of supersymmetry with compressed particle spectra.

We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by simulating the effect of material dispersion and solving the 3D cavity structure using the finite element method. Our simulations demonstrate an efficiency of approximately 90% at a wavelength of 920 nm and a higher efficiency beyond 90% at 802 nm due to diminished dispersion. Additionally, the design features a compact size, namely 300x300 x 5 $\mu$m, contributing to its suitability for integration with a straight grating coupler. This property enables effective single photon collection and collection efficiency optimization. This source type is预期 to enable precision quantum communication and quantum computing applications.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that provides insight into the nature of boson peaks through multiple approaches, including comparison of different scattering channels and analysis of temperature-dependent contributions. This technique has been enhanced by the development of new instruments and improved methods, enabling precise measurements down to very low temperatures of 0.35 K. These advancements have allowed for the discovery of subtle structural movements within glassy materials as potential origins for boson peaks, as well as the confirmation of their relationship with similar motions in liquids prior to crystallization. Moreover, the technique has identified universal patterns in glassy materials across different types and structures.

Particle physics is undergoing a transformation with the advent of a new theoretical framework, quantum field theory, which links theoretical calculations to experimental and theoretical data. Despite significant advancements, accurate predictions still pose a significant hurdle, especially with complex calculations involving multiple loops and scales. However, with ongoing advancements, exact predictions are within reach. In this context, we provide an introduction to the essential techniques and methods used for precision calculations, focusing on high-energy and extra-dimensional scenarios.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be seen in a galaxy map that shows emissions up to 60 kiloparsecs from the galactic center. A far-side component corresponding to this arm has been found in multiple tracers of star formation activity. This new far-side arm, located around 8-8.5 kiloparsecs from the center, is associated with significant inflow of neutral gas into the galactic plane, approximately 300 cubic parsecs per year, which may contribute to the formation of nearby star-forming regions.

Multi-objective optimization has become an essential approach for discovering a broad range of solutions to complex problems. This research builds on the concept of phenotypic diversity, initially explored in evolutionary multi-objective optimization, and extends its application to problems with multiple solutions. We present a novel framework that enables the clear visualization of phenotypic diversity, allowing for a direct and comprehensive assessment of different optimization methods. Through the analysis of two real-world cases, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework and provide an in-depth comparison of three optimization techniques, providing valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of each method.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem exist, such as the Three-Dimensional Stable Roommates problem, which adds constraints by requiring pairing a set of agents based on three distinct characteristics. A more complex version incorporates additively separable preferences to calculate the total satisfaction among the set of agents. A more in-depth analysis investigates whether a preferred pairings adhering to the constraints exist, and at what computational cost they can be found. A stable and optimal solution is defined as a pairings that is both stable among the set of agents and maximizes collective satisfaction. Results of the research reveal that finding a stable and preferred matchings, as well as optimizing stable and preferred matchings is a task achievable within a manageable time frame.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When we restrict
our study to conventional mechanisms, we discover that interatomic forces of
short range are primarily responsible for significant valley electron-phonon
coupling. In contrast, when we take into consideration other mechanisms, we
observe that spin-orbit interaction within the phonon mode can strongly affect
valley physics. Specifically, for phonon mode coupling to valence bands, we
identify a key factor as the energy gap between these bands. Our comprehensive
analysis provides valuable guidance for engineering valley electronic devices
based on two-dimensional infinite semiconductors and predicts potential
advantages of the abnormal electron-phonon coupling mechanisms.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured up to the Gromov-Hausdorff distance. This is done by considering the equivalence relation where two spaces are equivalent if their Gromov-Hausdorff distance is less than a fixed positive constant $\epsilon$. The equivalence classes, or "clouds," contain maximal sets of metric spaces with this property. Clouds exhibit a total ordering through the relation of continuous extension and one maximal element exists for each equivalence class. Furthermore, it is shown that this maximal element exists because every set of metric spaces with distance less than $\epsilon$ includes a space with the maximum possible diameter. Additionally, it is proven that extensions from the boundary to the maximum element exist not only for point sets but also for compact metrics and pseudometrics. A key finding is that any equivalence class has a unique "center" which is the metric space with the minimum "depth" within that class. It's also noted that the relations of continuous extension and minimal distance are directly linked to the concepts of Blashcke-Schnirelmann equivalence and Gromov-Hausdorff equivalence, respectively. These connections reveal new properties of these equivalence classes and their representative spaces.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates both the patch and feeding line efficiently. The angular range of the designed antenna is 160 degrees, achieved through a carefully optimized broadside orientation, thereby minimizing side lobes. The performance of this antenna has been thoroughly evaluated through comprehensive simulations and practical experiments, demonstrating substantial agreement, with the return loss measured at -17.66 dB, radiated phase and group delay matching within a 2% discrepancy, and the radiation pattern's experimental main lobe deviation falling within 2% of its simulated counterpart. The simplicity and low production cost of this antenna make it highly suitable for integration with other similar antennas in various applications, such as beam steering, frequency-swept radar, and cognitive radar systems.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, researchers successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models.

Quantum metrology enhances measurement precision using correlated states as sensors to detect weak signals like a small temperature difference between two systems. This work proposes an innovative method to simultaneously measure temperature variations between two cavities by employing an array of atomic qubits and monitoring quantum jumps triggered by an atomic probe. The temperature difference influences the cavity light's correlation properties, which are then amplified by the quantum jumb-meter through the cavity-atoms interaction. The approach can be implemented using existing quantum technologies and has been tested using a combination of theoretical and experimental data. By adjusting key parameters, one can optimize the method to achieve different levels of temperature resolution or achieve a relative temperature difference measurement precision of 0.01% within 60 seconds.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that Au$+$Au correlations diverge significantly from both $p$$+$$p$ and $d$$+$Au benchmarks. Notably, they exhibit reduced side and forward sector asymmetry and decreased hadron $p_{T}$ compared to $d$$+$Au collisions. These trends contradict predictions based on initial state effects alone, suggesting enhanced particle suppression in Au$+$Au compared to $d$$+$Au. This phenomenon can be interpreted as evidence of additional parton interactions in Au$+$Au, a phenomenon referred to as enhancement of shadowing saturation.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any arbitrary unitary operation is decomposed into a combination of natural processes occurring in quantum hardware and artificial operations provided by the hardware's control electronics. Building on this concept, we present a method to simulate fermionic systems, such as those found in chemical systems, using this digital-analog approach. The simulation utilizes a combination of variational quantum eigensolver and lattice fermion methods. We implement this method both experimentally on IBM quantum processors and through a high-fidelity quantum simulator. Notably, our research identifies specific advantages provided by both variational and lattice embeddings. The experiment's results show that the cost of each iteration in optimizing the quantum circuit can serve as a crucial indicator for choosing the most suitable lattice type. Furthermore, our lattice embedding strategy achieves an impressive reduction of 6 orders of magnitude in the depth of quantum circuits, a feature that could be particularly beneficial for achieving fault-tolerant computations in the future.

A common issue in machine learning models is the balance between optimizing performance and creating comprehensive features, known as the optimization-feature creation dilemma. Several methods have been developed to resolve related problems, such as overfitting and catastrophic forgetting. However, there has been little to no research addressing the optimization-generalization dilemma directly. In this paper, we introduce a new technique called RFC, which involves creating an intricate feature space with distinct regions for different generalizations. By using gradient-based optimization, RFC ensures that samples with the same label are grouped together and maintain stability. Our experimental results indicate that models built with the RFC feature space achieve superior performance on multiple datasets in various learning scenarios. Rich Feature Construction for the Optimization-Generalization Dilemma

Achieving the target light intensity to stimulate light-sensitive tissues or alter their properties while they're surrounded by tissue is challenging due to altered light propagation properties caused by tissue's optical heterogeneity. Direct methods often fail to produce clear images or deliver adequate power to the target area, and two-photon excitation is particularly sensitive to these changes. To address this, we developed an advanced algorithm for creating 3-D complex light patterns within highly scattering media. Our approach builds an algorithm similar to the consistent adjoint method but uses an iterative correction to form complex patterns simultaneously in different locations within the target area. To do this, we developed a flexible algorithm for controlling light with an external modulator and an adaptable complex amplitude phase mask to create desired light patterns within the area. Our results show that our algorithm can produce multiple excited sources in different locations within the area and maintain stability over time as the properties of the surrounding tissue change.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the narrow gap between anodes increasing series resistance. To overcome this drawback, we investigated the electrical properties of 375 μm thick LDCC and SOI sensors with various depths and underlying materials. With collection electrode depth being a key factor in drift resistance, we found that shallow positions favor a robust front end circuit, crucial for high-energy applications.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, which the standard Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process struggles to do effectively. We introduce a statistical approach to mitigate the limitations of the CIR model and investigate the potential advantages of our proposed model over the status quo. We evaluate and compare the model's intrinsic properties and demonstrate, through simulations, that our model improves the fit to real-world data. We also conduct an empirical assessment by testing the model on bond yield data and find that its incorporation yields a notable model enhancement.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the theoretical framework of scenario C as proposed by the DUNE collaboration. According to this scenario, DUNE has a 3-sigma discovery reach extending up to 0.1-1 GeV if certain conditions regarding sterile neutrino and proton decay thresholds are met. If conditions regarding sterile neutrino and proton decay are met, up to 10000 sterile neutrinos per year could be produced and detected. Our findings also indicate that the near detector of DUNE has substantial potential for searching into shorter baseline oscillations, a space currently occupied by experiments such as SBND and HD-NuB. Furthermore, the DUNE far detector has a role to play in searching into heavier sterile neutrinos compared to other dedicated experiments. Its ability to make contributions in these searches, however, depends on the achieved detection threshold for a given neutrino interaction cross-section.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes, which can arise due to interconnected outcome measures or variations in study designs and analyses.  Standard meta-analytic techniques, although straightforward to implement, may not adequately handle such correlations, potentially leading to underestimated standard errors and inflated type I error rates.  To address this issue, we compared cluster-robust standard errors with traditional methods in a comprehensive simulation study involving both real-world and artificially-generated data, which showed that the new approach provides more accurate inferences in scenarios with multiple correlations.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening time steps, but some options have proven unsuitable for specific types of collisions. We develop a numerical scheme that decouples collision and fluid dynamics time steps, ensuring stable and accurate simulation. Initially tested on simple collisions and flows with enhanced rates, the method is then applied to particle-resolved simulations of complex geometries and particle concentrations. Our results show the method's ability to efficiently handle particle collisions and reduce computational costs without compromising accuracy on particle-resolved simulations.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained via numerical analysis are then compared with LHCb and ALICE experimental findings for nuclear broadening in the context of J/Psi particles. Notably, models that align with small-x data are shown to yield transverse momentum variations consistent with measured values, especially for the specific cases of ALICE and LHCb experimental conditions.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed for ensuring consistency across HPX, a C++ template framework for parallel and distributed applications, by marking data with versioning and analyzing potential data dependencies prior to system crashes. The proposed method employs a dependency analysis based on code structure, circumventing the need for time-consuming runtime operations, and only requires the creation of versioning, which can be achieved through hardware support, without introducing additional overhead. The proposed approach relies on an analysis of data access patterns and code structure to identify potential dependencies, and does not rely on additional runtime operations. The proposed approach has been found to result in substantial reductions in data recovery times following crashes, particularly for large-scale applications, and has been shown to provide significant improvements in runtime efficiency.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present and navigate complex data collections, which has been the focus of research into automatic taxonomy generation. Existing methods for taxonomy extraction have come from the realms of data mining and natural language processing. The investigation of such systems is essential due to their applications in streamlined navigation, automated topic classification, and streamlined data management systems. This research aims to bridge the theoretical concepts of taxonomy formation and broader system design principles. Building on the concepts of Forming, Ranking, and Selection from organizational theory, we introduce the FRSC model. The novel model integrates these three operations and demonstrates their interdependence through theoretical examples. The paper showcases the practical usage of the model via a case study on the construction of a university course classification system, using a real-world dataset of course titles. The model's capabilities allow for the creation of a comprehensive course framework, accompanied by insights into the structure of the course network and its potential development patterns. The course hierarchies created through model's application provide a structured overview of the university's curriculum. The model's outcomes also reveal emerging areas within the system and areas where the hierarchy remains incomplete. The course classification system's construction illustrates the FRSC model's theoretical foundation, providing the underpinning for a range of additional research possibilities.

We conducted an experiment involving the statistical prediction of non-equilibrium systems using the N-body problem. The prediction method is based on the flux between distinct regions in the N-body phase space, and its validity is confirmed through direct comparison with direct N-body simulation results. A prediction method based on the flux between distinct regions in the N-body phase space, known as the Flux-based statistical prediction (FSPP), has been proposed for non-equilibrium systems with a limited number of particles. According to this approach, the time evolution of any particular sub-system can be expressed as a continuity equation. A complex system can be broken down into multiple simpler sub-systems, and the total system is characterized by the sum of these sub-systems. Within each sub-system, a simplified model is employed, and the interactions between different sub-systems are represented as fluxes. The interaction flux is calculated based on the boundary of each sub-system, and the total system is characterized by the sum of these sub-systems. Furthermore, we present our numerical results for the prediction of three-particle rings and the three-particle KAM torus systems, and we discuss the potential applications of FSPP.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors $R_{AA}$ for J/$\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ mesons were made in collisions with lead-lead at the Large Hadron Collider using data collected in 2015 by the CMS experiment. This research found that both prompt and nonprompt $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ mesons experienced suppression more severely than their higher mass counterparts, with suppression being more intense in high density environments. This study also demonstrated that the ratio of nonprompt to prompt $J/\psi$ remained unchanged under lead-lead collisions but was found to be lower than the prompt $J/\psi$ NMR factor.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, specifying its requirements can be challenging due to conflicting expectations, often resulting in an extensive list of requirements. Verifying if each requirement functions correctly and independently from others necessitates comprehensive testing with numerous test cases. However, running all test cases would be extremely time-consuming, both in setting up and executing them. Therefore, only a subset of selected test cases is executed, with retesting repeated runs eliminated. One such algorithm for test case selection using singular value decomposition, previously proposed, is now optimized for parallel execution. This revised version of the algorithm leverages modern multi-core processors to significantly reduce the overall testing time.

A novel approach to predicting suicidal ideation utilizes deep sequential models that analyze multi-source data, leveraging previous assessments and electronic health records. We employed a step-by-step methodology to construct these models, starting with individual recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for previous assessments, which demonstrated the capability to learn from previous test results and train effectively even in the presence of data imbalance. Subsequent models incorporated additional data, such as RNN-based analysis of medical records and combined datasets, which further enhanced predictive performance. Notably, the deep sequential model-based approach surpassed traditional machine learning models in terms of AUC and associated metrics. We emphasize the importance of transparency in training and evaluation methodologies to facilitate reproducible research in this field.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission from the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A using data from the IXPE observation. This discovery/polarization significance was obtained with an effective exposure of 28.7 ks. Our analyzed data supports a power law model with a spectral index of $1.34 \pm 0.13$ and no detectable cutoff up to 60 keV. This model aligns with prior observations from previous studies. Furthermore, our composite modeling of the source, featuring both power law and cutoff power law models, reveals polarization percentages ranging between 2.7% and 10.4% within the 3-20 keV energy band. This discovery indicates that the polarization percentage likely exhibits energy dependence, aligning with expectations based on synchrotron radiation theory. Data obtained from IXPE demonstrates that the polarization percentage strongly correlates with photon flux intensity, suggesting a magnetic field that aligns with particle propagation processes. This supports the notion of an ordered and likely aligned magnetic field that may be present within spherically structured shells.

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of $a_n$.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, remain poorly understood. The properties of this dense matter significantly impact the structure of compact stars. Present research aims to explore dense matter containing both electrons and compact quarks while maintaining equilibrium between them. Assumed is that this dense matter includes three flavors of quarks and maintains absolute stability against the decay of strange quarks. The used equations of state for the dense matter contain both a constant density approximation for the electrons and a charged Bag equation of state for the compact quarks. The generated equations of state enable the investigation of the sound velocity within dense matter containing stable quarks at densities up to approximately thirty times the nuclear saturation density. At such high densities, the sound velocity of dense matter exceeds the light speed. The generated equations of state match those that maintain bulk beta equilibrium between electrons and compact quarks within dense matter at zero temperature. The bulk beta equilibrium curve is bulk beta equilibrium between compact quarks at zero temperature. The bulk beta equilibrium curve is also compared to that calculated via a Lattice QCD lattice theory. Calculated is also the bulk beta equilibrium curve. The bulk beta equilibrium curve is then discussed in terms of the bulk beta equilibrium between compact quarks at zero temperature. We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent phase space characteristics.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are subject to irregular movement such as splashing and atomization, the resulting fluid structures can be intricate and embedded in their surroundings. Employing conventional interface representation methods with Lagrangian markers or Eulerian cells often leads to vast amounts of data and complex visualizations. The incorporation of a skeletal framework within a Eulerian framework mitigates this issue, thus significantly reducing the amount of necessary information and facilitating simpler visual representations. This research aims to study the internal dynamics of multiphase flows by analyzing the underlying structure of interfaces that form due to partial filling of control volumes.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by rolling along them, as shown in recent studies. This phenomenon was previously proposed to be an example of viral surface metabolism, where the collection of spike proteins interacts with the carbohydrates, generating mechanical movement through a self-organizing process. This research aims to investigate in greater detail the physical aspects underlying this rolling motion, developing a theory that explains the motor's behavior, as well as validating the results using simulations and analyzing experimental data. The results show that the motor's transition into this rolling state is driven by the formation of stable structures created by the spike proteins.

We examined over 5000 optical galaxy images from the SDSS database and discovered approximately 1700 "warped" disk galaxies, of which around 500 exhibited distinct features similar to the jellyfish galaxy J1252+63. Approximately 80 "warp" galaxies in close proximity to another galaxy, likely interacting with it, were juxtaposed with the jellyfish galaxy samples. This study explored various interaction aspects, such as tidal features, the relative positioning of the galaxy pair, and color differences, and we made comparisons with the JELLYFISH-SDSS project results. We observed that W galaxies, characterized by substantial interaction with the group/cluster, were found either near the cluster center or at the periphery, and those interacting externally showed characteristics of an external interaction, whereas those internally did not show clear signs of interaction and might represent "frozen" interactions during a passage through the cluster core. We noticed that JW galaxies, likely interacting with a companion, showed characteristics of an interaction and were found in a group with similar numbers to non-interacting warp galaxies. Furthermore, we observed that JW galaxies, along with other interacting galaxies, shared similar blue colors, while non-warp galaxies, despite being less affected by interactions, showed blue colors less frequently than non-interacting warp galaxies. This could potentially be a result of the intense interactions affecting JW galaxies, leading to starbursts and subsequent quenching in a short timescale

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic structures called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The arrangement of atoms within these crystals permits the existence of chirally behaving phonons, which correspond to atoms circling their equilibrium positions. Chiral symmetry results in a separation between the x and y coordinates, leading to momentum that is not conserved. We analyze a model featuring 12-atom unit cells, which represent a minimal structure necessary for the occurrence of chirality. This minimal structure, however, prevents linear dispersion and is therefore incompatible with light-matter interactions. We then investigate the dynamic behavior of the phonons, which may possess symmetry characteristics differing from those of the atoms composing them.

In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how the position of a nucleus affects free-charged carriers in band theory. We've generalized this concept to include metals, deriving formulas for three- and two-photon processes like the Hall effect and interband Conduction-Contrast (C/C) transitions. We show that in a time-reversal symmetric system, a simple expression for the Drude weight arises, connecting the band velocity to the overlap of core and conduction band wavefunctions. These findings have been validated by a simple model and our applications to Al and Pt reveal that the interband contribution to the Born effective charge can be as large as the core contribution.

We are re-evalu two key points as a group of researchers. Firstly, the concept of turbulence being driven by thermal noise at a certain frequency range in fluid mixtures is being scrutinized. This theory arises from the belief that thermal noise of large, chaotic flow patterns has significance within a particular frequency range. This claim is being challenged based on direct observation and analysis, particularly in terms of velocity measurements, non-invasive imaging, and theoretical understanding, all of which contradict each other. Secondly, at a different scale and range, the validity of applying the Kubo-Crank equation to fluids is being questioned. Analysis of frequency range and spatial range fluctuations follows the Khanin equation in these cases.

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric response characterized by a theta parameter of theta = pi. The phenomenon of magnetoelectricity is primarily responsible for several surface effects, including the Witten effect and an anomalous Hall effect. Due to the topological nature of these phenomena, they exhibit robustness. The non-linear response of magnetoelectricity is described by a specific tensor and results in both the Witten effect and the anomalous Hall effect being quantized with half-integers. The theta field theory is constructed to model the various effects arising from topological magnetoelectricity, including a couple-charge effect resulting from applying a magnetic field and an electromotive force generated by an electric field. Additionally, it showcases the quantization characteristics that define topological insulation.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's map exhibits mode locking, characteristic of laminar chaos. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of contexts, including planning, brainstorming, and problem-solving, often taking place in person or online. These conversations provide a wealth of information about how software projects progress, but their unstructured nature poses a challenge for automated analysis. As a result, current design mining techniques struggle to accurately predict system failures based on discussions, as different interpretations of the same phrases can significantly alter their underlying meaning. This research introduces the concept of conclusion stability to bridge this gap, offering a way to categorize discussions by the nature of their content. Building on this foundation, a set of semi-supervised learning algorithms is proposed to boost their performance in fault prediction. The approach is validated through a comprehensive case study involving a large software project from the Open Source Domain, where conclusions outperform traditional design mining techniques and outperform a baseline algorithm. Notably, rules generated by this approach provide actionable insights into development processes, contributing to a better understanding of system failures.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent aspects of a quantum field.
Gravity emerges from the exchange of virtual photons between electrons and false vacuum state components, facilitated by the exchange of gluons between these components, which also accounts for the majority of the proton's mass, thereby linking dark energy to the majority of the proton's mass.
The exchange of virtual photons exchanged between electrons with false vacuum state components exerts the force that we recognize as gravity.
A theoretical framework, which may provide a solution to the hierarchy problem, also describes the force mediated by the W and Z bosons.

Proximal methods are effective in minimizing non-smooth, constrained optimization problems.
The corresponding unconstrained problems often result in manifolds that are generally difficult
to identify due to the absence of an explicit formula, making a direct feasibility check impossible.
To address this issue, we propose an algorithm that projects optimization variables onto the optimization
manifold at each step using Newton's method, akin to an embedded algorithm. Nonetheless, we note that
such projects require explicit formula for the optimization manifold, rendering them impractical in many cases.
Instead, we utilize proximal methods that only need infeasible penalties of the constraint function, provided
they can be approximated by sub-linear rate. The proximal operator can be found by solving a related
unconstrained optimization problem that results in a manifiold-parallel one.
To address this issue, we formulate a problem that identifies the optimal approximation using the
Newton's method and the proximal operator is identified in a few iterations.
The algorithm is applicable to a wide range non-smooth optimization problems including
minimum phase error over complex unitary matrices and optimal form-fitting.
We demonstrate the performance of the novel algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art methods.

We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a, b, c$ in $R$ and any element $d$ in $I$, the product of $a, b, c, d$ is contained in $I$ implies that $d$ belongs to $I$ or the product of $a, b, c$ is contained in $I$. This concept generalizes the notion of $1$-absorbing prime ideals. Several of its inherent properties and related theorems are studied, which establishes its relationship with other special prime ideals. Additionally, rings with specific types of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals, such as plinbian rings, thin prime rings, $1$-prime rings, and weakly $1$-absorbing principal ideal domains, along with certain examples, are examined in further detail.

We present new findings for two semileptonic decay processes, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, utilizing data from Belle II's sample, containing 1.5 exaflops of computational processing power from the 2019-2021 run. By employing the hadronic decay products of the opposing $B$ meson, our analysis uses 42.6 $b^{-1}$ integrated luminosity. Through the use of matrix element likelihood analysis, our results reveal total signal counts of 2370 and 1336 for the $B^0$ and $B^+$ decay processes, respectively. Consequently, our measurements indicate total and differential decay rates for both processes, divided into three distinct q^2 ranges, determined by the squared momentum between the two decay products.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with ripples that mirror those in desired filter profiles. We combined two device platforms - silicon carbide and indium gallium phosphide - to create custom template spectra by fanning out specific wavelengths and then filtering them according to required profiles. Our innovations include photonic devices with performance comparable to the highest-end commercial instruments in astronomy. These inventions enable planetary transit searches to be completed in a single exposure by performing cross-correlation on-device. Furthermore, these technologies offer limitless scalability and customization capabilities.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

Several approaches have been implemented to identify and evaluate road conditions in order to assist transportation officials in making informed decisions about budget allocation and policy development. Traditional methods of damage detection involve manual inspections by trained personnel and have specific applications for collecting and analyzing data. Nevertheless, these approaches have limitations in accurately recognizing complex road conditions and are time-consuming and expensive to implement on a large scale. The advancement in deep learning technology has facilitated the use of automated road condition analysis using images, but most studies to date have been confined to evaluating performance on a single dataset. This research aims to address this limitation by proposing a transfer learning-based deep convolutional neural network model that can accurately detect various types of road and runway damages in images. The research also seeks to overcome the challenges associated with developing such models by addressing issues related to domain and style transfers across multiple countries, a task that has been challenging due to a lack of standard protocols. By comparing the proposed model's results with those obtained from conventional image processing techniques and existing deep learning approaches, the research demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed model in accurately identifying road damages across different domains.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation learning techniques often rely on direct access to expert demonstrations.  These demonstrations provide valuable insights into the ideal actions that expert agents take, but extracting this information can be complicated when full state-action pairs aren't available.  In cases where only observational data from experts is available, it becomes even more challenging since these demonstrations do not accurately reflect the actual actions that experts take.  Moreover, it becomes impossible for these observables to be used in a different environment if they were learned from a different one.  UDLT addresses these complexities by using a novel system that learns to simulate and perform like an expert from available observational data, and then transfers this expertise across varying environments to allow for generalization.

A major uncertainty surrounds the initial massive Population III stars and their subsequent disc environments. Our research focused on the magnetic influence during this phase. We analyzed magnetic field dynamics around a forming Population III star at the edge of their surrounding disc using state-of_theart simulations that incorporate magnetic field amplification processes. Specifically, the simulations showed an extremely rapid increase in magnetic field strength due to the accumulation of magnetic flux at the dense region near the star's surface. As the flux accumulated, the magnetic force began dominating over gravity in this area, leading to a rapid expansion of the disk and redistribution of matter outward. This effect eliminated fragmentation in the disk around these early stars for an extended period, regardless of initial conditions.

This research focuses on two key aspects of association rules: redundancy and a new concept called minimum-size bases. It also introduces the idea of deduction schemes to preserve meaningful association rules during data mining processes that involve reducing existing datasets. A specific type of deduction scheme is proposed - one that aims to retain all important association rules within data subsets while ensuring the smallest possible number of association rules within those subsets. One instance of this concept is examined, along with its relationship to hyperplane removal deduction schemes. Various computational methods are proposed for determining minimum-size bases for association rules.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health issues.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or approximately 13 percentage points.  The positive results were most evident when mental health treatment as part of the sentence was contrasted with no such treatment, and were consistent across various crime types and levels of severity.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip unmanned aerial vehicles with the capability to wirelessly charge their counterparts on the ground, which could be made possible by an easily accessible and widely distributed aerial network of free-spectrum frequencies. However, gathering the necessary data for radio maps poses a significant challenge, largely due to the uncertainty of ground-based electronic interference patterns and the limitations of existing UAVs' hardware. These constraints significantly hinder the uncertainty reduction process, making it difficult to accurately assess and predict electronic interference patterns. In this context, our research aims to overcome these obstacles by proposing a new, ground-based electronic interference detection method that leverages the synergistic effects of smart data collection methods and advanced data analysis techniques to accurately build radio maps, all while using minimal resources. Our proposed method begins with observing and adapting to collection paths that effectively broaden the diversity of gathered data without requiring predefined plans. Subsequently, we employ a novel extension of Gaussian process regression, which takes into account the uncertainty in measured data to further refine gathering strategies by strategically selecting optimal locations for data collection at each step, thereby accelerating the development of radio maps. In order to validate our approach, a new hardware platform with advanced features was built, which uses a compact, space-efficient design and a resource-efficient signal processing method to generate accurate data despite limited onboard resources. This hardware was then deployed on the ground to collect data, which revealed that our developments enable feature-rich radio maps to be generated within a very short period of just one day

This paper outlines a novel approach for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series using Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). It builds on a frame-based anomaly detection technique, incorporating an additional step of using an HMM to determine the probability distribution of frame lengths. Unlikely samples are identified if either an HMM or the distribution model produces a low probability score for a given sample. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a simulation of equipment failure in a power system, featuring a 25-day interval irregular maintenance schedule. Our results show that combining the two detection methods significantly improves overall anomaly detection performance.

This research delves into a variety of aspects of person verification using audio-visual and thermal images. We study a number of data sources and design a modern neural architecture that uses a combination of these modalities for better verification. We explore the effectiveness of fusion techniques and analyze the impact of a number of network components on verification accuracy. We also develop and report a new thermal-image-based verification model and a combined audio-visual-thermal Person Verification system, achieving SOTA results on a comprehensive benchmark.

Generating new training data through augmentation is achieved by manipulating existing data. We compare two methods, including time-stretching, for training speech recognition and translation models. Increasing the amount of speech recognition training data by 26% using time-stretching led to a comparable score to that of the baseline, without increasing the computational cost. Also, adding back-translation to the training speech translation pipeline resulted in a small improvement in score while maintaining a similar computational cost. Overall, increasing the amount of existing data through time-stretching has the least impact on computational costs while yielding the greatest benefits.

An unknown distribution of the form $\pi(\theta)$ has an associated expectation, represented as $\psi^\pi = \int_\Theta \psi(\theta) \pi(\theta) d\theta$. Now, suppose we have random observations, represented as $Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_{n_1}, \ldots, Y_{n}, \ldots$, where, for each $n$, the observations $Y_{(n-1)+1}, \ldots, Y_{n}$ are independently and identically distributed according to $\theta_n$, and the $\theta_n$ values are independent and drawn according to the distribution $\pi$. If the observations $Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_{n}$ are available, the goal is to find a consistent estimator for the expectation $\psi^\pi$.
