Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena such as nontransitive dice and the 52/23 puzzle, a novel class of distributed models has been developed, simulating a race between two players, $A$ and $B$, who draw numbers from separate distributions, $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$. The game's outcome hinges on whether the number $r$ that is drawn more frequently exceeds $q$, the number that is drawn oftenest. The research investigates the conditions under which, for any $\mu_B$, there exist $\mu_A$ probabilities that make $P(A \text{ wins}) > P(A \text{ loses})$ or that the win/loss probabilities are equal. Furthermore, a novel class of cyclic probabilities has been introduced, demonstrating existence through concrete examples, while a potential application of the research in teaching nontransitive dice is outlined.

Many software systems have adjustable settings through run-time parameters, such as the number of threads in a simulator. However, these configurations also have fixed aspects determined before the system is built, such as the threading model, which significantly impacts performance. An optimal system configuration requires identifying and testing multiple possible settings to ensure the system performs well across different environments. This process is time-consuming and consumes resources due and prone to human error. Our proposed approach simplifies this process by automatically optimizing system performance through the adjustment of both fixed and changeable configurations. Currently, there are not many existing techniques that can effectively specialize systems considering both types of configurations. In this study, we investigate the potential benefits of an automated approach that replaces adaptable system components with specialized, performance-optimized versions. Our analysis reveals significant improvements in performance and reductions in file size using our proposed technique. Moreover, our data supports the view that compile-time specialization results in performance-optimized systems without the need for further runtime optimization. Ultimately, this study contributes to the field by validating the value of compile-time specialization for both configurations that can be adjusted and those that are fixed.

Light dark matter particles like sub-GeV $Z'$ mediators can transfer a considerable amount of energy through elastic collisions with atomic nuclei, generating electron recoil signals that are detectable. This process offers a more efficient and media-accessible way of detecting such particles compared to previous methods focused on photon emission from target nuclei. A new approach combines this potential with existing direct detection experiments to establish stringent limits on sub-GeV $Z'$ mediators. By using a simulation-based technique, we demonstrate the effectiveness of combining the potentials of various nuclei in conventional direct detection experiments, and we project significantly improved constraints on sub-GeV $Z'$ mediators. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of utilizing a greater variety of mediators that couple primarily to quarks and lepton number. Our research also includes an examination of systematics that might limit the effectiveness of this approach.

This paper investigates entanglement, rapid swing of Rabi oscillations and quantum communication within the anti-Jaynes-Cummings system, examining entanglement, state transfer and related phenomena under various initial conditions. We trace entanglement's evolution over time, utilizing a conditional average of the Meyer-wallman measure to quantify it. Our investigations into entanglement, state transfer and Rabi oscillations in the anti-Jaynes-Cummings system reveal significant parallels with the standard J-C model.

Non-invasive estimation of respiratory and cardiac rates is achievable by analyzing external cues such as audio and visual data obtained from various sources like cameras and microphones. Effective monitoring systems rely on accurate non-invasive estimation of cardiac rate and inter-beat intervals, which can be challenging due to diverse heart conditions and individual variations. In this research, a novel technique was developed that involves accurate estimation of non-metric inter-beat intervals from electrocardiogram signals, which was then transformed into a metric distance function, and finally utilized to calculate the current inter-beat interval, all without being affected by past beats. Our approach's performance was evaluated and compared against existing methods using data from public databases and experimental data, demonstrating superior results and lower errors.

We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confinement. Analytical calculations of the rate function are done using a saddle-point approximation. Additionally, numerical simulations validate these findings. 
By examining how an active force impacts work fluctuations, our results show an asymmetry in the fluctuation spectrum and a modification in the fluctuation amplitude. 
Interestingly, as external entropy is introduced, our data on active and passive particles in a harmonic oscillator reveal a striking difference, 
namely an unusual, highly localized enhancement around zero work values, indicating that active forces can perform and extract work in probabilistic excess. 
These findings demonstrate that active forces significantly impact work fluctuations and Exergy production and have profound implications for understanding how energy is distributed and controlled.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across a range of subjects. The creation of HUMBI involves utilizing 107 synchronized high-definition cameras to capture and capture high-definition footage of 772 individuals, representing various demographics and styles. Using these multi-view images, we apply advanced 3D mesh modeling to accurately reconstruct and analyze diverse human body expressions from multiple viewpoints. The proposed dataset demonstrates exceptional efficiency in learning and reconstructing three-dimensional human body features, surpassing existing methods in primary tasks like unsupervised unskeletonized mesh generation, unsupervised skeleton estimation, and pose classification by significantly improving overall results. The HUMBI dataset is freely accessible via https://humbi.cs.uh.edu.

Despite the growing success of multilingual pre-trained models, their application to resources with less abundant data remains challenging due to data scarcity and annotation costs. We propose an innovative, minimal-supervision approach leveraging task representations from high-data languages for low-data languages, specifically targeting the noun phrase challenge. By leveraging existing rich data among languages, our method circumvents the limited resource constraint without requiring data augmentation or retraining, and integrates a new, efficient data modification technique called residual representations. Comprehensive evaluations on multiple datasets and models demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent model, which uses alignment and enhancement modules to exploit spatial-temporal information from input frames. The "basic VSR" model, an improvement on earlier recurrences, utilized the last output as its own hidden state to enhance performance. However, it only incorporated two modules, often failing to utilize valuable information from older frames. More recently, the "BasicVSR" model took inspiration from recurrent neural networks and self-attention, yet it was prone to error propagation, a problem that undermines many such models. In an effort to address these issues, we have further optimized the basic VSR model by introducing several key modifications, including a novel module to propagate features across multiple time stamps, which helps to use even remote historical information, and an additional alignment module to incorporate structural features from multiple hidden states, thereby reducing error propagation. Experimental results on the DMPEG and film REC images demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by a considerable margin and achieving an impressive PSNR of +0.33 dB on RecVideo.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using a shared policy can be beneficial
as it allows previous tasks' achievements to contribute to subsequent ones,
effectively preventing problems of performance degradation and knowledge loss
that often arise from severe interference. However, using a single network to
represent multiple tasks increases the risk of severe interference and
compromises individual task representations. To address this, we propose a new
approach where each task has its own network module within a modular network
structure, preventing tasks from overwriting one another while still allowing
computationally efficient re-use of module outputs for novel tasks. We demonstrate
the advantages of our method in both synthetic and real-world learning scenarios
by showing it significantly reduces interference and enables successful
transfer between tasks in multi-task robotic manipulation experiments.

We have improved the performance of heat engines working within specific timeframes and subjected to restricted adjustments. These limitations include evenly distributed changes in temperature and bounded alterations in energy storage capacity. Our analysis shows that engines using exponential changes in temperature outperform those using linear profiles. Moreover, within these specific constraints, the optimal shape of the heat engine cycle cannot be determined without additional constraints on work output. However, meaningful results can be achieved by fixing the work output and developing an approximate optimal cycle. A analogous outcome is achieved for heat engines with no constraints on control.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To achieve this, we develop a statistical representation of wind pressure distributions that accounts for the probabilistic nature of both hurricane paths and storm surges. In addition, we create a dynamic model of real-time power supply and demand in each zone of the grid that accounts for the cumulative effect of weather-related disruptions. This model enables us to calculate the probability of excessive load and the potential system collapse resulting from weather-induced in disruptions. The framework we propose is applied to the Eastern Interconnection power grid to assess vulnerability to hurricane-derived wind and storm surge stress. The framework can be adapted to assess potential financial losses and physical damage to power infrastructure in the grid.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages and combinatorics. Leveraging weak-rotation coding, we derive a mechanism for the non-approachability of entropy in cases where the set of stable directions has co-dimension greater than one.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately explains all observed phenomena or if there are additional components lurking within the scalar sector. A comprehensive theoretical framework predicts a multitude of new particles emerging from this expanded scalar sector, each with the potential to be discovered through diverse decay pathways. This review delves into the prospects and strategies for discovering these elusive particles at future colliders such as the Nucleon-Large Ion Collider (NCLIC) and the e+e- collider (e+e-).

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) designed to synthesize one-dimensional signals with controlled pitch and duration. Traditional WaveNet has limitations when generating periodic signals due to the reliance on simple fully connected layers and the linear relationship between frequency and duration. To overcome these challenges, we proposed QPNet that incorporates pitch-dependent dilated convolutional layers, PDC, replacing the standard fully connected layers. The QPNet structure utilizes a U-Net design with skip connections between up and down sampling operations to improve frequency resolution for longer frequencies. Experimental results show that the QPNet model outperforms traditional WaveNet in generating periodic signals, particularly for higher pitch lengths.

The approach to collaborative filtering using biclustering has shown great potential, and we believe that the Bicluster-based CF (BcCF) method can become a comprehensive solution. To date, BcCF research has primarily focused on enhancing coverage by addressing the issue of relevance sparsity. However, the issue of preference locality has not been adequately addressed. To develop a full-solution BcCF approach, this paper presents three BcCF variants that address three crucial concerns: (1) preference sparsity, (2) preference locality, and (3) subjectivity in ratings. The first variant filters out noisy and irrelevant data to improve accuracy by addressing sparsity, while the second utilizes biclusters to identify and remove user-specific similarities that indicate local preferences. To combat rating bias, the third variant employs biclusters and transforms numerical ratings into categorical data. Extensive tests using realistic data sets confirm the high performance of BcCF, and the results show that BcCF outperforms established CF techniques, particularly in addressing the challenge of relevance sparsity.

Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these effects from planetary signals using high-precision radial velocity data. By analyzing the HARPS-N observations of the Sun over eight years, we aim to pinpoint indicators of magnetic behavior that reflect the spectral impact of activity spots, which are responsible for most spectral distortions. Comparing this research to similar studies of stellar activity will also provide valuable insights. We examined the radial velocity variations across a wide spectral range and found some discrepancies between models of stellar activity and actual data in the UV, visible, and infrared spectra. While most radial velocity indicators show similar patterns, we discovered an anomaly in the infrared that reflects the seasonal variation of chromospheric activity levels. Additionally, we developed a method to identify the spectral features of spots that shift spectral energy distributions and determined their significance in the HARPS-N spectral range.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, we suggest an experiment where the sample is accessed via electrodes with significant resistance, causing Ohmic dissipation, as supported by recent research by Zhang et al. According to our analysis, Ohmic dissipation produces a zero-energy peak in the second derivative of conductance that becomes more prominent at lower temperatures and higher impedance ratios between the sample and electrodes. Notably, this effect is more pronounced with smaller electrode sizes and more resistive electrodes. Another key distinction is that a Oyster-type system with homogeneous broadening does not exhibit such a peak under these conditions. Additionally, this method does not be affected by magnetic disorder.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes from a single input, while others get trapped during iterative optimization and struggle with inconsistent styles across images, requiring repeated retraining for each new style. To address these challenges, our method employs a pair of images for tone mapping, leveraging a pre-trained neural network trained on the CelebaStyle dataset, which provides accurate target outputs for a given original image. By using this paired data, our model can distill the style from image pairs, ensuring consistent outcomes while avoiding repetition issues. Furthermore, our technique enables the transfer of the learned style to unpaired images, demonstrating effective style transfer on the CelebaStyle and ImageNet datasets.

This technical report showcases the winning solution of our model for the LOVEU AQTC competition, which received a first-place ranking at CVPR 2022. Our approach involved generating high-quality annotations for images, which were then used to train a pre-existing pre-trained model. The resulting annotations showed exceptional accuracy, showing only minor discrepancies compared to the ground truth. Additionally, we achieved a top-ranking score of 0.0825 in mAP for car categories and an impressive mean 3D bounding box results score of 0.8436.

This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmosphere's turbulence and snowflake behavior during snowfalls. A state-of-the-art imaging system is utilized to capture snowflakes in action while measurements of turbulence are taken with a portable equipment, termed SODAR. Research indicates that snowflakes tend to concentrate in regions of intense turbulence and downward motion, suggesting the existence of snowflake aggregation processes and an associated phenomenon called preferential sweeping. Furthermore, researchers discovered that smaller snowflakes are more susceptible to being trapped and denser flakes show less concentration.

A significant hurdle in developing autonomous navigation systems for service robots is the need to connect high-level task descriptions with real-world environments where the goal is to maximize a desired outcome. Many existing approaches rely on pre-defined tasks and a limited set of perceived states for the purpose of control, which falls short of addressing complex, unfamiliar environments with a wide array of states. In contrast, Proactive Active Inference has emerged as a promising solution by providing a unified framework that encompasses perception, prediction, and decision-making processes to effectively navigate through various states in order to maintain a desired level of comfort. However, applying this method to a robot requires that it first learn the patterns of free spaces, but the number of possible states is vast, making traditional reinforcement learning impractical. In an effort to create a general-purpose navigation system, this research presents a novel Deep Active Inference method that integrates active learning to improve the efficiency of training by selecting the most informative samples, and uses a novel loss function to accelerate the process. The proposed method has been successfully demonstrated in a robotic platform that integrates deep reinforcement learning and active learning for the purpose of learning, adapting, and navigating in free space environments while the goal is to maintain a desired outcome. The performance of the Deep Active Inference algorithm outperformed traditional reinforcement learning algorithms in terms of sample efficiency and computational efficiency.

In experimental environments, Track Pattern Recognition (TPR) plays a pivotal role in analyzing experimental data by identifying and matching track segments. While utilizing track patterns in data analysis enhances its trackability, the vast amount of sparse 3D data generated can severely limit performance due to processing complexity. To address this issue, an effective data compression technique specific to sparse patterns is crucial. Existing compression methods employing convolutional neural networks face challenges in efficiently processing sparse patterns. To overcome these limitations, a new data compression technique using a Bicephalous Convolutional Autoencoder (BCA) is introduced, designed to efficiently compress sparse patterns using the patterns themselves as reference points. Thorough testing of the proposed BCA-based compression technique using TAO demonstrates its superiority over current state-of-the-art compression techniques, yielding a 4.47 times higher compression ratio at an equivalent 95 per cent recovery rate. Furthermore, the incorporation of proposed compression into the TAO detector yields minimal per-view processing time increase of 0.004666667 seconds.

Utilizing Finzi's gravity theory that enhances interactions at large scales, we analyze galaxy clusters from a thermodynamic perspective, establishing a statistical model to derive thermodynamic equations and comparing clustering behavior with Newtonian gravity. We also explore the general distribution function's behavior as the clustering parameter varies in strength, with the finding that phase transitions are feasible, albeit hierarchically organized.

A type of convex geometric hypergraph, known as cgh, comprises a set of subsets originating from strictly convex point sets in the plane. In this study, researchers explore a specific type of problem associated with cghs: saturation problems that correspond to earlier studies on extremal problems. These problems had been initially addressed for specific cases, and the current study examines a specific type of cgh saturation problem by examining a specific graph where the edges connect vertices in the plane in a way that forms convex quadrilaterals. The study proves a specific theorem regarding the edges in the graph where any saturation for the given number of vertices in the plane results in the edges forming the triangles in the plane, and the study establishes a specific numerical value representing the maximum number of edges in the graph where the edges forming the triangles in the plane, and the study explores the geometric properties of the saturated configurations and their relationships.

To gain a better understanding of the relative contributions of different processes, the angular distributions of alpha particles resulting from elastic, inelastic, and fusion reactions were measured as a function of energy for the 6Li + 51V system. Experiments were conducted to identify and distinguish among these alphas, and the data showed that 6Li + 51V inelastic reactions dominated over other processes within the measured energy range. Notably, the experiment-found angular distributions matched theoretical IQM predictions. Furthermore, to quantify the impact of low-energy cutoff on cross-section calculations, the 6Li's in-depth distribution was also recorded and found to significantly contribute to reactions. Consequently, reaction cross-sections were revised and a comparison with energy-dependent system estimates revealed an overall slight underestimation by the latter.

A previously overlooked ability in bio-inspired swimming systems is the capacity to climb vertical surfaces. The anadromous Pacific Lamprey utilizes a unique locomotion technique when migrating between the ocean and freshwater habitats. A notable part of their journey involves navigating steep rivers and climbing straight, vertical surfaces. By studying their natural strategies, researchers have introduced a novel ability to robotic vehicles. The complex combination of forces that enable the Pacific Lamprey to climb has been replicated on a robot, involving the creation of vortices through surface undulations and manipulation of water currents.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework.

Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on effective scheduling decisions, which have been explored through various approaches mainly focusing on enhancing energy efficiency or minimizing interference, often neglecting the timeliness of data delivery. Successful data transmission relies not just on high data rates but also on timely delivery within a device's Data Age of Information (AoI). Prioritizing minimal AoI, we investigate the design of an optimal scheduling policy in a D2D system, consisting of an auxiliary D2D pair and $N$ regular D2D pairs with fixed routes. To address the complex and high-cost nature of the optimization problem, we develop an iterative algorithm that achieves the minimum AoI sum. To tackle the computational limitations associated with the real-time implementation of the proposed algorithm, we introduce a deep learning context-aware scheduling (DCAS) algorithm, employing a Convolutional Neural Network to predict the optimal device pairs for each context, thereby reducing signaling overhead and AoI, with demonstrated effectiveness in in-car scenarios.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [25] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic, compressible flow with smooth solutions. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to this system in a specific mathematical space ensure the conservation of helicity. Additionally, similar results were found for both homogeneous incompressible Euler equations and the surface quasi-geostrophic equation.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations, focusing particularly on the large spectral parameter $k$ in a specified reference \cite{KlSjSt20}. They now examined how this work can be applied to the reflection coefficient and derived new asymptotic formulas for specific domains with potential functions and smooth, strictly convex boundaries.

Researchers have established that initial assumptions that orbits of merging binary systems remain plane during flight may be inaccurate. To investigate this, they developed a new analytical framework for calculating how the orbital plane's eccentricity evolves in systems that become more or less eccentric over time. Starting with an almost circular orbit, the model determines the remaining orbital eccentricity when a binary system enters the frequency range of gravitational wave detection. By integrating precise mathematical expansions of orbital responses, the authors obtain detection thresholds for various orbiting masses and spin configurations. For LIGO detectors, they find that for typical stellar-mass black hole mergers, orbits can retain an eccentricity as low as 0.003 to 0.02, depending on source distance, which offers a motive to model and model the effects of orbital imperfections on observed wave patterns in these scenarios.

A proposed X-ray coherent amplification technique, based on a free-electron laser oscillator and seeded by an external laser, is being explored to generate high-intensity X-ray pulses. By integrating and modulating the laser mode in a free-electron laser oscillator using diffraction grators, a checkered photon field with controllable spatial features can be created and amplified in an interaction chamber. Amplification leads to the emergence of distinct laser modes at specific frequencies. Using tailored quadrupole magnets, the X-ray beam can be focused, yielding an intense, mode-filtered X-ray beam. A key benefit of this technique is its ability to produce an intense X-ray beam with controlled temporal and spatial characteristics.

Event detection on dynamic graphs is a crucial task across various domain events.  The goal of detecting significant state transitions in instances over time where each instance comprises multiple nodes is achieved.  Graphical Process Algebras emerge as a primary approach to address this issue,尽管 maintaining the temporal order of nodes is essential, traditional GPAs fail to capture this feature.  In this study, we incorporate a characteristic unique to each node - its time stamp - into the standard GPA model, enabling explicit representation of the temporal order.  Furthermore, we introduce a novel non-deterministic GPA for precise detection of events, demonstrating detection capabilities on a set of synthetic and real-world datasets.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show how these theoretical solutions can be accurately reproduced in Lagrangian hydrodynamic simulations, thereby validating and verifying these codes for a range of scenarios.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties.

Characterizing colorectal polyps endoscopically and surgically requires pathologists to evaluate them based on multiple levels. The first assessment involves distinguishing between benign adenomas, which require further analysis to determine the presence of dysplasia. Adenoma classification helps assess malignancy risk and guides medical treatment. We present UniToPatho, an annotated dataset of histological slides of colorectal polyps, enabling deep learning models to identify adenomas and classify dysplasia. The dataset includes 1,666 H&E images and 85,752 segmentation masks, supporting segmentation, classification tasks. The proposed dataset and associated findings appear in the paper.

In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The adversary attempts to deduce a topologically embedded property of the source distribution. We model the adversary's capability by defining a non-identifiable structure, which could represent a two-dimensional structure such as a circle or square. This structure is embedded within a probabilistic framework consisting of a simple graph representing all possible sources. We establish a fundamental limit on the adversary's potential gain by deriving the maximum mutual information between the encoded message and the discovered property. This is achieved by introducing a randomized encoding scheme, akin to a local anti-plethropic cover. We show the case for circular embeddings in three-dimensional distributions and analyze how the embedded dimension influences the adversary's potential gain in both circular and square scenarios.

Deep learning-based methods have shown great potential in enhancing the resolution of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images. However, current methods have limitations in resolving fine details that are not present in low-resolution images. Researchers have therefore proposed a new approach, a MrSARP model, which stands for a multi-resolution sparse auto-radar prior in the frequency domain. The MrSARP model combines a hierarchical deep generative prior with sparsity in the SAR image's S-transform domain to improve high-resolution restoration. A deep generative prior is trained to map coarser SAR images to a higher-dimensional latent space and then generates high-resolution images based on the captured low-resolution image information. The MrSARP model employs a hierarchical generator network to produce detailed images, while the first-order Markov model captures global structure within the latent space. A conditional sparsity transformer is used to estimate the sparse coefficients in the MrSARP model, which then serves as a loss function for refining the generated images. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the MrSARP model in producing high-resolution images with clearer and more realistic structures. The model outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of PSNR and SSIM scores and produces visually superior outcomes.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm's early stages utilize a parameter-encoding approach that often requires a costly quantum experiment-based method to optimize its parameters.  A novel quantum-classical optimization strategy called Bayesian Optimization has shown promising results in optimizing these parameters, ultimately outperforming alternative methods.  With the ability to handle complex, discontinuous functions and account for experimental data uncertainty, Bayesian Optimization seamlessly integrates data and theory in a rigorous manner.  This work investigates the effectiveness of Bayesian Optimization in optimizing the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm's parameters.  The results show that Bayesian Optimization surpasses alternative methods on a range of test problems of increasing difficulty, providing substantial energy improvements on difficult test cases and marking the first successful large-scale application of Bayesian Optimization in quantum approximation-based optimizers.  The implementation provided here serves as a comprehensive reference for researchers and educators in the application of Bayesian Optimization to quantum approximation-based optimizers.

A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The Gauss-Shohne formula serves as the foundation for calculating these segment areas, resolving a previously unsolved problem. The algorithm utilizes the roots of a degree four polynomial to identify up to eight intersection points and employs an adaptive angular sampling scheme to identify the points' relative positions, thereby calculating the overlap area. Notably, when one ellipse degenerates into a circle or a line, the algorithm accurately calculates the corresponding overlap areas. The performance efficiency is highlighted when there are no intersection points, as the algorithm requires at most eight and two root calculations for this scenario.

Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we expand the framework by incorporating non-stationary environments and actions that are defined continuously. To address the complexity that arises from continuous time and actions, we adopt a linear parameterization, incorporate a sampling interval and a function approximation, and then examine the convergence as the time interval approaches zero. In doing so, we develop an online algorithm that learns the parameters of a q-function through direct linear inverse problems. Ultimately, this algorithm drives the agent towards the solutions of Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) equations.

Quantum magnetism on triangular and honeycomb lattices is a key area of research for understanding magnetic properties in materials. We investigate the effect of second nearest neighbor interactions on magnetic fluctuations within a Hubbard model on a triangular lattice using numerical simulations. These simulations focus on the behavior of spin waves in small systems using exact linear spin wave theory and dynamic mean field theory, applying it to square lattice Hubbard model predictions. Results show significant effects of antiferromagnetic interactions on spin fluctuations and that considering interlayer interactions within the square lattice model leads to a more accurate representation of magnetic behavior than purely triangular or collinear models.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial for numerous clinical applications and treatments like radiotherapy and surgical planning. However, certain certain localization and identification methods are hindered due to poor visibility of the vertebral boundaries in CT images. In this study, an advanced deep learning-based approach is proposed, which utilizes a spinal image transformation technique to create clearer views of the vertebral structures. The proposed model also incorporates a specialized cost function that takes into account the anatomical relationships of the vertebrae, which aids in enhancing and stabilizing localization and identification of the vertebrae. The evaluation of the proposed method involved a comprehensive dataset of 1,200 CT scans, which were compared against the current best methods through evaluation of the detection and identification accuracy. In addition, the identification accuracy was assessed within specific body regions, which revealed notable gains over the baseline methods. Finally, a semi-automatic radiotherapy tool development was initiated, which will benefit from the proposed framework.

Stochastic thermodynamics offers a framework for analyzing heat and work in systems driven by external forces and subjected to random fluctuations. A key concept within this framework is the joint probability of heat and work, from which the efficiency of energy conversion can be determined. However, traditional stochastic thermodynamics suffers from inherent inconsistencies in defining efficiencies, due to various choices of general forces and extended variables. These shortcoming can lead to diverse and often conflicting conclusions regarding the efficiency of energy utilization. To address these issues, we introduce a joint probability distribution specific to the system's boundary, allowing for the precise measurement of current flow. Utilizing this framework, we show that asymptotic averages of current and efficiency are independent of external parameters, providing clear and consistent results. As a practical application, we re-examine a model of a Brownian motor and derive the precise asymptotic statistics of its current and efficiency.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy across an intervening vacuum gap by transmitting acoustic waves. Our research provides a mathematical explanation for how this energy transfer occurs and reveals that specific conditions allow for complete transmission of these waves. Through a detailed analysis of the acoustic field around the materials, we derived an expression that can be used to calculate the energy transfer and found that it can be accurately modeled without considering thermal effects. Our findings show that when the materials are cut in certain ways (specifically, along their radial axes) and have particular electrical and mechanical properties, they can transmit acoustic energy across vacuum gaps as small as tens of nanometers with near-100% efficiency. This energy transfer is based on a combination of two fundamental parameters and can potentially be used to develop advanced technologies for measuring sound waves. Our study validates these predictions by examining zinc oxide materials, showing that they can facilitate complete energy transfer across vacuum gaps of up to ~300 Å, and potentially be applied more broadly to other piezoelectric materials, such as zinc and gallium doped materials.

We explore a cutting-edge method for producing optical patterns known as reservoir optics, which utilizes an alternative source instead of the traditional object, in experiments involving polariton condensates. By transferring the responsibility for forming images to the reservoir, this method relaxes constraints on polariton optics for producing structured light. Since discoveries of polariton condensates have been made in 2008, various experiments have been conducted to produce images of obstacles located in front of the sample using polariton condensates. However, conventional methods for image formation are limited due to difficulties in maintaining polariton coherence and producing polariton condensates at room temperature. Since room-temperature operations are crucial for practical applications of polariton condensates, our research presents a novel approach where patterns formed within the reservoir itself in response to an external pattern are used as the object for further coherent light scattering by the exciton-polariton condensate that produces the final image. Specifically, our experiments involve an optical pattern placed within the reservoir, in conjunction with an exciton-polariton condensate that forms within the system in response to an excitation laser. Our results show that scattering of polariton condensates can produce images of optical patterns and demonstrate correlations consistent with nonlocal behavior of polariton condensates. Furthermore, our research opens up new possibilities for the production of room-temperature structured light in various applications.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns of debris clouds and a decreasing lifetime, prompting a need to examine the properties of its dusty tail and the dynamics of its disintegration process. Despite various hypotheses, current models are insufficient in explaining the complex dust characteristics observed, prompting a comprehensive analysis through observations and simulations. To this end, we combined post-formation disk modeling, hydrodynamic simulations, and radiative transfer simulations to evaluate the efficacy of two distinct mass loss processes at a range of masses and sizes of dust particles produced as the exoplanet disintegrates. Our study found that a high mass loss rate of approximately 10^-10 solar masses per year and a high probability of exponential disintegration with a mean lifetime of a few million years best explain the system's properties. Moreover, our study determined that a range of particle sizes and distribution of dust sizes from 0.1 to 10 microns are present, dispelling earlier assumptions that limit dust particle sizes to a few fractions of a micron.

We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffeomorphism of the Milnor fibration remains unchanged within each category.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this library accommodates both imperative and object-oriented programming methodologies. Its comprehensive toolkit encompasses data framing, cleaning, statistical analysis, machine learning capabilities, and visualization functions. Developed to complement existing.NET data science resources, the Daany library emphasizes transparency, enabling users to easily understand and replicate its analytics processes. A key feature of Daany is its ability to generate and interpret explanatory models through visualizations, thereby addressing a previously unmet need in.NET data analytics. The library's abilities can be categorized into four main areas: data framing, cleaning, statistical modeling, and the development of machine learning models. Its full source code, documentation, and examples are freely accessible on GitHub.

I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's contribution to science, which centers on his use of experiment and mathematics to study nature, by arguing that his work was rooted in medieval natural philosophy. This philosophical framework, rather than a limitation, facilitated Galileo's transition from natural philosophy to modern science, as it was integral to his understanding of how to investigate the world through mathematics and experiment.

The increasing popularity of Hailey-Smith distributions among cosmologists stems from their simplicity and the ease of comparing nested models. In this study, a new parametric form for the distribution is introduced to more accurately capture Saha ionization dynamics. A subsequent numerical analysis confirms that the proposed model effectively reproduces Saha evolution across a range of frequencies and temperatures. Furthermore, a novel approach to calculating blackbody entropy and specific heat using the new distribution is presented, revealing significant deviations from standard Bessel function calculations at high frequencies, particularly in terms of phase shifts and amplitude variations. These analytical results serve as a useful starting point for investigating non-standard ionization dynamics in the early universe.

The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes a hybrid approach, incorporating the magnetohydrodynamics with adaptively embedded particle-in-Cell model, to investigate the reconnection of two magnetic fields at an X-line interface through coalescence. By matching the scales of the magnetic fields and gradually advancing the interfaces, our simulations incorporate kinetic effects and observe a gradual transition into a laminar coalescence coalescence state, followed by the emergence of a distinct shock coalescence structure characterized by two separate interfaces. Despite varying initial conditions, our simulations follow the same coalescence process, exhibiting an asymmetric coalescence phenomenon on the interfaces and an increase in reconnection rate at early stages, whereas late-stage, the phenomena becomes less prominent. Our findings, although indicating that kinetic effects can be observed in MHD simulations, suggest that the observed phenomena could also be the result of numerical artifacts.

This document introduces the Amanuensis project, a pioneering AI system designed to accelerate software development by providing intelligent completion of complex code snippets. Unlike traditional tools, Amanuensis is specifically tailored to support programming languages like C++ and Kotlin within the Android ecosystem. The system functions as a virtual development partner, predicting the full methodology required to solve a problem based on the user's initial code input. As users' coding habits evolve over time, Amanuensis learns to personalize its completion suggestions to seamlessly adapt to the developer's individual working style. This learned knowledge enables Amanuensis to anticipate coding needs proactively, thereby reducing the cognitive load on developers and enhancing overall productivity through a collaborative AI-driven approach to software development. The Amanuensis project aims to revolutionize software creation by transforming AI into intelligent allies for professional developers.
